Title: SaaS Data Moats: Why Proprietary Data Is the Strongest Competitive Advantage in 2026

URL Source: https://www.saasmag.com/saas-data-moats-proprietary-competitive-advantage/

Published Time: 2026-08-21T09:48:12+00:00

Markdown Content:
## SaaS Data Moats: Why Proprietary Data Is the Strongest Competitive Advantage in 2026

On February 3, 2026, public SaaS valuations lost roughly [$285 billion in a single trading session](https://www.taskade.com/blog/saaspocalypse-explained). The market repriced an entire category of software companies whose primary moat was development time. AI-assisted development had compressed that advantage from years to months, and Wall Street noticed.

But not every SaaS stock cratered equally. Companies sitting on proprietary data assets, the kind competitors cannot replicate by hiring faster engineers or licensing better models, recovered within weeks. The ones still trading below their January highs six months later are disproportionately the thin-wrapper tools with no unique data layer.

The lesson is blunt: in a world where anyone can build comparable features using the same foundation models, the SaaS companies with durable competitive advantages are the ones accumulating proprietary data that compounds over time. This is the data moat, and it is rapidly becoming the single most important factor in SaaS defensibility and valuation.

## The Moat Conversation Has Shifted Permanently

Designli’s [2026 Moat Report](https://designli.co/founders-resources-blog/the-moat-report-how-saas-founders-are-building-defensibility-in-2026), a survey of 100 SaaS founders and operators, reveals a telling contradiction. Custom AI and machine learning models are the single most-cited technical differentiator, named by 35.7% of respondents. Yet proprietary integrations, unique infrastructure, and founders who say their edge is not technical at all each tied for second place at 21.4%.

The contradiction matters. Founders overwhelmingly believe AI is their moat, but the AI itself is built on commodity models anyone can access. The actual moat is not the model. It is the data the model trains on, and whether that data improves with every customer interaction in ways a competitor starting from scratch cannot match.

Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy put it plainly at [Snowflake Summit 2026](https://www.alation.com/blog/snowflake-summit-2026-takeaways/) in June: models give you zero competitive advantage because your competitors can buy the same ones. Your proprietary data is what creates the real advantage. More than 20,000 attendees heard that message, and it reflects what acquirers and investors have been saying privately for over a year.

![Image 1: SaaS Founder Technical Differentiators 2026 Survey](https://www.saasmag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/chart-1-saas-data-moats-proprietary-competitive-advantage.png)

Source: Designli 2026 Moat Report — SaaS founders’ most-cited technical differentiators

## What Actually Qualifies as a Data Moat

Not all data creates defensibility. Storing customer records in a database is table stakes, not a moat. A genuine data moat has three characteristics: the data is domain-specific enough that generic datasets cannot substitute for it, it is longitudinal (accumulated over months or years of real usage), and it is tied to measurable outcomes that make the product demonstrably better.

Consider how this plays out in practice. [CRV’s 2026 AI-native guide](https://www.crv.com/content/what-is-ai-native) identifies the compounding data flywheel as the single best indicator of a defensible AI moat. If your AI improves with use because it learns from proprietary customer data that no competitor has access to, that advantage widens over time. If your AI is just calling the same API as everyone else with no proprietary training data, you have a feature, not a moat.

Datadog illustrates the distinction. Its observability platform ingests telemetry from over 32,700 customers’ production environments, according to [recent competitive analysis](https://artificall.com/analysis/companies/comparisons/datadog-vs-snowflake/). That telemetry powers anomaly detection models trained on patterns across thousands of infrastructure configurations. A new entrant can build a comparable dashboard, but it cannot replicate years of production telemetry from enterprise-scale deployments.

## The Data Flywheel: From Storage to Compounding Advantage

The concept is straightforward. More users generate more data. More data trains better models. Better models improve the product. A better product attracts more users. Each rotation of the flywheel widens the gap between the incumbent and any competitor attempting to catch up.

92% of SaaS companies have launched or plan to launch AI features, according to [2026 SaaS benchmark data](https://developmentcorporate.com/saas/2026-saas-benchmarks-the-ai-monetization-gap-ma-buyers-are-missing/). But only 29% currently monetize AI directly, and 67% of B2B SaaS companies with AI functionality do not charge incrementally for it. That gap reveals an uncomfortable truth: most companies are bolting AI onto existing products without the proprietary data layer that would make those features genuinely differentiated.

[Snowplow’s analysis of data flywheels](https://snowplow.io/blog/what-is-a-data-flywheel) breaks the mechanism into concrete steps. First, you capture behavioral data from core product usage, not just clicks but context-rich signals about what users are trying to accomplish. Second, you feed that data into models that personalize the experience. Third, the improved experience drives higher engagement, which generates richer data. The companies where this cycle spins fastest, think HubSpot’s CRM predicting deal outcomes or ZoomInfo’s B2B graph refining contact accuracy, are the ones building genuine separation from competitors.

## How Data Moats Drive Retention and Valuation Premiums

The financial case for data moats runs through net revenue retention. [ProductQuant’s 2026 NRR benchmarks](https://productquant.dev/blog/nrr-benchmarks-saas/) show a stark gradient: enterprise SaaS with ACV above $100K hits a median NRR of 118%, mid-market ($25K to $100K) lands at 108%, and SMB (below $25K) sits at 97%. Higher ACVs typically correlate with deeper data dependencies and higher switching costs, which is exactly what a data moat creates.

The valuation impact is dramatic. Companies with NRR above 120% trade at roughly [9.3x EV/revenue, compared to 3.1x for those below 100%](https://livmo.com/blog/saas-valuation-multiples-2026/). A 10-point NRR increase can boost valuation by 20 to 30 percent, according to [Value Add VC’s analysis](https://valueaddvc.com/blog/why-net-revenue-retention-is-the-single-biggest-driver-of-saas-multiples). That premium reflects the compounding math: a company with 120% NRR and $10 million in ARR grows its existing customer base to roughly $24.9 million over five years without acquiring a single new logo.

![Image 2: SaaS NRR vs Valuation Multiples 2026](https://www.saasmag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/chart-2-saas-data-moats-proprietary-competitive-advantage.png)

NRR tiers and their corresponding EV/Revenue multiples in 2026

Contrast that with AI-native tools that lack data moats. [ProductQuant reports](https://productquant.dev/blog/nrr-benchmarks-saas/) that AI-native SaaS tools with low switching costs posted a median NRR near 48% in late 2025, with sub-$50 per month plans at just 32% NRR. When customers can replicate your functionality with a prompt, there is no data gravity holding them in place. The [retention math is unforgiving](https://www.saasmag.com/net-revenue-retention-defining-saas-metric/).

## Five Patterns That Build Real Data Moats

After reviewing the Designli survey data, benchmark reports, and how top-performing SaaS companies structure their data strategies, five patterns stand out.

### 1. Workflow Data Capture at the Point of Action

Every user interaction becomes a training signal. Figma accumulates design-pattern datasets through core product use. Notion captures knowledge-organization workflows. The key distinction: this data is generated as a byproduct of the user doing their job, not through a separate data-collection step that adds friction.

### 2. Proprietary Benchmarks from Aggregated Customer Data

Companies like ChartMogul and Paddle anonymize and aggregate customer data into industry benchmarks that become valuable standalone products. This creates a secondary moat: customers stay partly because leaving means losing access to the benchmark context that informs their own decisions.

### 3. Network Effects Through Data Sharing

Snowflake’s Marketplace and Native Application Framework let customers share, purchase, and monetize datasets directly on the platform. Each participant adds data to the ecosystem, creating a network effect that a single-tenant competitor cannot replicate. [API-first SaaS companies](https://www.saasmag.com/api-first-saas-winning/) are particularly well-positioned here because each integration adds data surface area.

### 4. Domain-Specific Compliance Data

In regulated industries like healthcare, finance, and legal, compliance data creates a moat that is difficult and expensive to replicate. The switching cost is not just the software migration. It includes re-validating compliance workflows, re-training staff on new audit trails, and the risk of gaps during transition. Vertical SaaS companies in these sectors routinely post [annual logo churn below 5%](https://www.saasmag.com/vertical-saas-niche-beats-horizontal-2026/).

### 5. Feedback Loops That Visibly Improve the Product

This is the pattern that separates data hoarding from a genuine data moat. Every data asset must connect to a visible product improvement. If customers cannot see their data making the product smarter, the data is not functioning as a moat. It is just storage cost.

## The Caveat Most Founders Miss

Designli’s survey found that founders are building moats reactively, responding to competitive pressure as it appears rather than designing for compounding advantage from day one. Roughly 14% of respondents admitted they were not placing any differentiated distribution bet at all.

Data moats also fall apart in specific conditions that rarely appear in pitch decks. If your data governance is weak, meaning you cannot demonstrate to enterprise buyers exactly how their data is handled, stored, and anonymized, the moat dissolves into a liability. Privacy regulations are tightening globally, and a data asset you cannot prove compliance for is a write-off, not an advantage.

There is also a scale threshold. A data moat only works when you have enough data density to produce measurably better outcomes than a competitor with access to public data. For most B2B SaaS products, that threshold requires hundreds of customers in a specific vertical generating data for 12 or more months. Below that threshold, you have a data collection, not a moat. Founders who claim a data moat at seed stage with 30 customers are telling a story, not describing reality.

One more caveat for operators running at scale: the [AI COGS problem](https://www.saasmag.com/ai-cogs-saas-gross-margin-compression/) applies directly here. The more you invest in AI features that consume your proprietary data, the more inference cost you absorb. Gross margins for LLM-native companies sit around 65%, according to [a16z’s analysis](https://developmentcorporate.com/saas/a16z-the-saas-moat-scorecard/), well below the 80 to 90% ceiling that defined the prior decade. Your data moat must generate enough value to justify the margin compression.

![Image 3: SaaS Data Moat Strength vs Gross Margin](https://www.saasmag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/chart-3-saas-data-moats-proprietary-competitive-advantage.png)

The relationship between data moat strength and gross margin in AI-native SaaS

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a data moat in SaaS?

A data moat is a competitive advantage created when a SaaS company accumulates proprietary data that makes its product measurably better in ways competitors cannot easily replicate. Unlike feature-based differentiation, which AI can compress to months, a data moat compounds over time as more customers generate more domain-specific data. The moat is real when the data is longitudinal, tied to outcomes, and feeds directly into product improvement. Companies with strong data moats typically show higher NRR, lower churn, and command premium valuations.

### How does a data flywheel create competitive advantage?

A data flywheel works through a self-reinforcing cycle: more users create more data, more data trains better models, better models improve the product, and a better product attracts more users. Each rotation widens the gap between the incumbent and new entrants. The advantage compounds because a competitor starting from zero cannot replicate years of accumulated, domain-specific usage data by simply building a similar product. The flywheel must be deliberately designed into the product architecture, not bolted on afterward.

### Which SaaS companies have the strongest data moats?

Companies frequently cited for strong data moats include Snowflake (data marketplace creating network effects), Datadog (production telemetry from 32,700+ customers), ZoomInfo (proprietary B2B contact graph), and HubSpot (CRM interaction data powering predictive features). Vertical SaaS companies in healthcare, legal, and financial services also build deep data moats through domain-specific compliance and workflow data that horizontal competitors cannot easily replicate.

### Data moat vs. network effects: what is the difference?

Network effects increase product value as more users join, while a data moat increases product quality as more data accumulates. They often overlap but are distinct. A marketplace has network effects (more buyers attract more sellers) without necessarily having a data moat. A vertical SaaS tool might have a data moat (years of compliance records making predictions more accurate) without network effects. The strongest competitive positions combine both, where more users generate more data, and that data makes the platform more valuable for everyone.

### How do data moats affect SaaS valuations in 2026?

Data moats drive valuations primarily through their impact on net revenue retention. SaaS companies with NRR above 120%, often enabled by high switching costs from data dependencies, trade at roughly 9.3x EV/revenue versus 3.1x for those below 100%. AI-native SaaS with proprietary data commands an additional 30 to 50% valuation premium over comparable non-AI peers. Acquirers in 2026 are explicitly paying for data depth and workflow lock-in, discounting feature-based moats that AI can replicate.

## Building the Moat That Matters

The SaaS companies that will command premium valuations through 2027 and beyond are not the ones building the flashiest AI features. They are the ones quietly accumulating proprietary data assets that compound with every customer interaction, every workflow completed, every data point generated.

The playbook is clear but requires patience. Capture data at the point of action. Build feedback loops that visibly improve the product. Aggregate insights that create standalone value. Design switching costs around data gravity, not feature lock-in. And monitor the unit economics closely, because the margin implications of AI-powered data moats are real.

After February’s $285 billion correction, the market has made its preference unmistakable. Code is increasingly commodity. Distribution can be bought. But proprietary data that makes a product genuinely better with every passing month cannot be shortcut. That is the moat worth building.

Title: Served vs Seen: Which Brand Are You? | LBBOnline

URL Source: https://lbbonline.com/news/The-Efficiency-Trap-Jon-Reeves-VaynerMedia

Published Time: 2026-08-21T08:05:33.063+00:00

Markdown Content:
_Jon looks at how an industry built around impressions, potential reach and efficiency metrics can create the illusion of effectiveness, while real consumer attention and ultimately business growth tells a different story._

_From media measurement and wastage to the role of creative and organic testing, he argues that brands need to stop treating delivery as proof of impact and start building around what actually earns attention._

_Because being served is only an opportunity to be seen. The brands that win will know the difference._

Corporate scrutiny of marketing budgets is on the rise. We all feel it.

In 2026 we've sat across from CFOs sharing the same concern: the marketing machinery they're funding isn't delivering business growth.

They're seeing reports full of positive metrics, while business performance continues to stagnate or slide.

What’s behind this?

A lot is being written about marketers caught in the efficiency trap of optimising towards the assumed safety of short term metrics, instead of embracing the perceived risk but proven reward of long-term brand building.

CMOs and their teams are being boxed into a corner by quarterly earnings reports, reaching for the metrics they know they can immediately move.

They are forced to justify their work in a fraction of the time needed to deliver long term growth.

The result?

Marketing performance on paper is becoming increasingly disconnected from driving business outcomes.

So, what can be done?

### **We Need A New Model**

That's the headline of the first slide we show when we meet with brands.

It was prompted by our proprietary meta-analysis of published studies from Binet & Field, GroupM/WARC, DataReportal and WFA/Ebiquity which points to an alarming trend.

Since 2019, marketing efficiency has increased by 63%, driven by programmatic & AI ad buying. In the same period brand growth, market share and long-term profit gains have fallen by 26%.

It’s the result of brands stuck in a campaign-led, media-locked annual model which is geared to win more with spreadsheets than with real people.

This traditional approach is no longer fit for purpose. Companies need a marketing model that acts as a growth driver rather than a money furnace.

At [Vayner](https://lbbonline.com/companies/vaynermedia-london/), everything we do is judged by its ability to drive business outcomes. Our approach is built around the reality of where consumer attention lives today and what consistently earns it.

So where should brands start if they want to change?

### **The Potential Reach Fallacy**

When I joined Vayner four years ago I remember Gary framing a flaw in marketing lore which has stayed with me ever since.

He remarked that most paid advertising is potential reach. Ads can be served in the desired medium at scale, but many are never actually seen and remembered. Where a one in a spreadsheet could well be a zero in real life.

That gap between potential reach and actual attention becomes more apparent when you start to pick at the systemic failings in our media ecosystem. For example:

1. A paid impression is counted as billable if 50% of an ad's pixels are on screen for as little as one to two seconds. (MRC & IAB guidelines)

2. Long-established principal-based trading practices prompt important questions around transparency, incentives and conflict of interest from leading media suppliers. (Project Claridges)

3. An evaluation of 20 million Smart TVs found that 8% to 10% of all CTV streaming impressions are delivered while the physical TV screen is turned off, wasting over $1 billion annually. (GroupM iSpot.tv / Doubleverify)

4. An analysis of $123M in ad spend across 35 billion impressions showed 21% of all programmatic impressions went directly to Made-for-Advertising (MFA) sites aka clickbait inventory engineered purely to farm ad impressions. (Association of National Advertisers)

5. Eye-tracking data reveals that 85% of digital/CTV ads fail to hit the 2.5-second active attention threshold required to generate brand memory, with 60% of commercial breaks playing out while the viewer's eyes are locked on a secondary mobile screen. (Prof. Karen Nelson-Field, Dentsu & TVision)

### **Media Amplifying Weak Creative Is Just Scaled Indifference**

Beyond these media fissures, poor creative is compounding the issue with audiences at scale tuning out when they feel they’re being sold to.

Who needs an ad blocker when we've trained ourselves to subconsciously swipe when we detect an 'ad'?

In today's algorithm-driven landscape, no amount of media can force people to spend time with creative they find irrelevant or uninteresting.

When the lion’s share (at times 80%) of marketing investment is being channelled towards potential reach and ineffective creative, brands are betting the farm on being served instead of being seen.

We believe in the alternative: grow brands by earning and scaling real attention. For advertising to do its job it has to be noticed, consumed, felt and remembered.

Advertising itself comes from the Latin advertere – 'to turn toward.' The ability to deliver effective promotion can only be achieved by brands who are actually being seen.

### **How to move from Served to Seen**

So how do you step off the hamster wheel of potential reach and poor creative? It starts with making better integrated decisions across creative, media and investment.

The emerging brands who are challenging category titans, are scaling what they have proven to already work. Out-operating when they can’t outspend.

For us, that proof lies in social. Specifically, identifying winning organic social creative via algorithmic distribution and flowing it directly into the brand’s hero media plans.

Marketers are living in the golden age of creative testing. We have free access to algorithms which the most valuable companies on the planet have spent billions of dollars training to deliver relevance.

We can road test creative with real audiences at scale before committing a single dollar of media investment. If content earns organic distribution at scale, it's our strongest signal for relevance because it will only scale if it is actually being consumed by real people.

Once creative has proven its relevance, paid media becomes an amplifier rather than a rescue plan. Instead of using media to mask weak creative, it scales ideas that have already demonstrated their ability to earn attention.

This significantly reduces marketing guesswork and corporate risk, placing investment behind a model geared to eliminate wastage and combat the unavoidable leakage within bought media.

The fastest growing brands today aren't simply buying more impressions. They're earning more attention by creating advertising people are choosing to spend time with.

These brands refuse to pot-commit until they have demonstrated their ability to earn attention and win over consumers.

Every marketing budget can buy one of two things.

The capacity to be Served.

Or the ability to be Seen.

The businesses that will come out on top over the next decade will understand and master the difference.

Stop paying to be Served. Start working to be Seen.

# Marketers, The Free Token Lunch Is Over. Is Your Stack Ready?

By Jon Morra, Zefr

Monday, August 24th, 2026 – 12:35 am

 SHARE: 

[LinkedIn](https://www.adexchanger.com/#linkedin)[Email](https://www.adexchanger.com/#email)[X](https://www.adexchanger.com/#x)[Facebook](https://www.adexchanger.com/#facebook)[Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.adexchanger.com%2Fdata-driven-thinking%2Fmarketers-the-free-token-lunch-is-over-is-your-stack-ready%2F&title=Marketers%2C%20The%20Free%20Token%20Lunch%20Is%20Over.%20Is%20Your%20Stack%20Ready%3F%20%7C%20AdExchanger)

![Image 5: Jon Morra, chief AI officer, Zefr](https://www.adexchanger.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/JonMorraHeadshot-scaled-e1712204780903.jpg)

Jon Morra Chief AI Officer![Image 6: Zefr logo](https://www.adexchanger.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/ZEFR_Logos_Charcoal_011916_aw_v1-1.png)

Anthropic just dropped[Claude Sonnet 5](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-sonnet-5), reigniting a broader debate about how AI should be priced. Some [argue](https://the-decoder.com/claude-sonnet-5-continues-anthropics-pattern-of-hiding-price-increases-behind-unchanged-token-rates/) that published token rates no longer tell the full economic story because changes in token consumption and model behavior, such as the use of reasoning tokens, can materially affect real-world costs.

Meanwhile, other alternatives like Fable 5 are priced at twice Anthropic’s prior top-tier model and no longer treated as unlimited plan features. Regardless of where you land in that debate, it’s becoming clear that the economics of AI are changing. Not to mention the[actual, ever-changing pricing structures.](https://www.computing.co.uk/news/2026/ai/anthropic-changes-pricing-structure-again)

Most companies running AI-powered marketing tools are not ready for what this means. They built their systems assuming both tokens would stay cheap forever and the number of tokens needed to achieve an outcome would stay flat.

![Image 7](https://www.adexchanger.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/advertisement2.png)

For years, AI builders and buyers have been rewarded for a pretty simple strategy: use the biggest model you can get your hands on. That worked while the cost of the hardware needed to run the models stayed within budget. It was easy to assume that more intelligence was always the right answer, but when you have to consider the cost of that intelligence, that is not always the correct, economical choice.

Now marketing needs to pay attention because this changes the conversation and the questions that marketers should be asking about their AI tools.

## **Matching model to task**

Think about the kinds of decisions AI is making across advertising today. Is this video suitable for a family-friendly campaign? Does this creator align with a brand’s values? Is this creative likely to violate a platform policy? Important questions, but they aren’t the same as asking an AI model to solve a complex legal problem or [prove cutting-edge math problems](https://physicsworld.com/a/ai-led-solutions-of-erdos-problems-spark-debate-over-the-future-of-mathematics/).

Ramp, which tracks AI spending across tens of thousands of businesses, found that although the average cost per million tokens has fallen dramatically over the past year, AI spending continues to climb for two reasons: breadth and depth. On the breadth side, companies are using AI to solve far more problems than they were a year ago.

On the depth side, most modern AI models now ship with [reasoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reasoning_model) enabled by default. Reasoning uses many times more tokens to “think” about answers to problems before generating the actual output tokens that respond to the prompt. Cheaper tokens didn’t lower AI budgets; they encouraged organizations to consume many more of them, a classic case of [Jevons paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox).

We are shifting back to unit economics, and marketers need to start looking at right-sizing models to the problems they actually need to solve.

Researchers are also beginning to evaluate AI in a different way. Instead of asking how much a token costs, they’re asking how much it costs to get the right answer. [Researchers recently proposed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13359?utm_source) a framework they call “cost-of-pass,” which measures the expected cost of producing a correct result. They concluded that different kinds of models are economically optimal for different kinds of work. Lightweight models excel on simpler tasks, larger models on knowledge-intensive ones and reasoning models earn their keep only when the problem is complex enough to justify the additional cost. My colleagues and I also [studied](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07006) this concept under the brand-safety paradigm, asking when to trust model outputs or escalate decisions to more expensive human review.

That’s exactly where I think enterprise AI is heading. We’re relearning that solving billions of repetitive decisions efficiently is a very different engineering challenge from solving one extraordinarily difficult problem. For engineers like myself, it can be challenging to overcome our[shiny object system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiny_object_syndrome). But when a technology needs to work at scale, we must.

Per-token price for frontier models may go up or down, but the cost to solve complex problems is going to increase. Anthropic won’t be the last lab to make that move. The question every marketer should be asking their AI vendors this quarter isn’t “Which model do you use?” It’s “Why does every task get the same model?” If the answer is habit rather than architecture, that’s where the next invoice surprise is coming from.

Title: “Thanks for your quick response”

URL Source: https://seths.blog/2026/08/thanks-for-your-quick-response/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T09:03:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
That’s pretty new. Letters sent by Thomas Jefferson from France often took months to get a response. No points for shaving a day off a 90-day correspondence lag.

The 800 toll-free number shifted the dynamic we expected from marketers. If we call you, we expect you to answer. Now, not later. FEDEX did the same for physical items–yes, of course I absolutely want it here tomorrow.

The race for speed doesn’t often have economic justification. I can probably live without a return label or customer service or some rabbit chow for a few minutes or even a few days…

But it’s the thought that counts.

If you’re not selling a commodity at the lowest price, that’s what you’ve got to sell. The thought.

Stories are built on a foundation of thoughtfulness, the empathy of seeing where the others are, what they dream of and what they fear.

And ‘quick response’ is one of the cheapest and most reliable ways to demonstrate that empathy.

Title: Behind Jack in the Box’s push into collectibles

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/jack-in-the-box-collectibles-brand-strategy

Published Time: 2026-08-24T10:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Would you purchase a meal for a collectible? Or wake up early to stake out a coffee shop for a limited-edition cup? Or stand in line for hours to get a pastel-colored grocery bag?

Whether it’s Starbucks and its Bearista cup, Trader Joe’s and its coveted tote bags, or [even movie theaters](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2024/11/22/how-the-specialty-popcorn-bucket-is-helping-build-out-the-theater-experience) with specialty popcorn buckets, brands are increasingly betting that creating collectibles can get consumers in the door. Sometimes collectibles come in the form of [a blind box](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2025/08/26/brands-blind-box-strategy-labubu-le-crueset-cava-lol-surprise), where the buyer doesn’t know what they’re getting until they open it, while other times, the item is publicized as a limited release to create a sense of scarcity—and, likely, [high resale value](https://www.yahoo.com/news/article/starbucks-apologizes-after-bearista-cup-sparks-fights-long-lines-and-500-resale-listings-191508172.html).

This year, the fast-food chain Jack in the Box, which is celebrating its 75th anniversary, is joining in on the collectibles craze. The QSR chain’s new line of collectible items, including glass Jack Sipper Cups shaped like its brand mascot, pins, and Labubu-like Jibbis bag charms, were inspired by a nostalgic collectible item it used to offer: an antenna topper featuring its mascot that was first distributed in the ’90s, Sheena Dougher, VP of brand marketing at Jack in the Box, told us.

For the brand, the offerings go beyond celebrating its anniversary. Dougher said the collectibles provide a way to meet changing guest expectations as “the value equation shifts” between brands and consumers.

“People want more for their money, and it goes beyond the food,” Dougher said. “They want experiences from brands.”

## **Expected experience**

The latest iteration of collectibles, the second edition of the Jibbis, rolled out earlier this summer as a companion to Jack in the Box’s Philly cheesesteak Munchie Meal. So far, the collectibles, which have also included antenna balls as “a nod back to the original,” have come as a gift with the purchase of one of the meals as the chain has looked to “elevate” the offering, Dougher said.

That said, the chain has also started to experiment with “actual solo purchases of the items.”

Get marketing news you'll actually want to read

Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides.

Dougher said the collectibles help to provide an experience that customers “not only want but they’re starting to expect;” the sweet spot, she added, is when the chain can make finding collectibles into “a game where you’re on the hunt to collect” all of them, or make something “extra rare” that “makes people so excited about these and why it was really important for us to be part of.”

For marketers, there can be other perks, too, whether that’s appealing to the growing “[kidult](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2025/07/24/labubus-hot-wheels-kidults-market-growth)” audience looking for an experience that reminds them of their childhoods, or tapping into [little-treat culture](https://adage.com/article/digital-marketing-ad-tech-news/gen-z-little-treat-culture-influences-glossier-dove-diet-coke-marketing/2605176/) popular among Gen Z. Another plus of the growing love of branded collectibles is the content creation that can come out of it: when a brand creates collectibles, there’s a chance that consumers will take photos and videos, whether it’s an official unboxing or just showing off the item on social media.

“At the end of the day, you’re gonna get all this content from nano [influencers] and micros [influencers],” Danielle Wiley, founder and CEO of Sway Group, told us.

That’s been the case for Jack in the Box and its Labubu-like Jibbis in particular. Fans of the charms have posted about seeking out the ones they’re missing, complete sets, and potential menu hacks to help with collecting.

While virality isn’t a guarantee, those posts can go a long way for brands looking to cut through the noise, Wiley told us.

“I think anyone who can jump into this is going to because all these brands need just so much content right now,” she said. “You’re gonna get content from doing that.”

kept.heading: INSTAGRAM SAYS CAPTIONS MATTER. THE REAL SHIFT IS CONTEXT (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The caption is no longer supporting copy on Instagram: it is becoming the context layer that tells people and search engines what a post actually means. The same photo could be a new release, an archival find, or a personal memory, and the caption is what tells the difference once content travels beyond a creator's own followers. Public posts from professional accounts can now be indexed by external search engines, so captions increasingly shape how content gets found.
kept.article_text:
Title: Instagram Says Captions Matter. The Real Shift Is Context

URL Source: https://wersm.com/instagram-captions-context-search/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T20:55:51+00:00

Markdown Content:
Instagram’s latest advice is not really about writing longer captions. It is about making visual content easier for people and machines to understand.

For a platform built on pictures, Instagram suddenly has a lot to say about words.

In [new guidance shared with creators](https://www.instagram.com/p/Db_N-P6kbt2/), Instagram argues that captions add context, encourage conversation and help search engines understand what a post is about.

Its practical recommendations are familiar enough: start with a strong opening line, tell a story or provide useful information, include a clear call to action, use relevant keywords and make longer text easier to read.

Instagram also recommends adding individual descriptions to carousel slides, a feature the platform [began testing earlier this year](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/instagram-tests-captions-on-each-post-within-carousels/819917/).

None of that sounds revolutionary.

Taken together, however, the advice points to a much more important shift.

The caption is no longer supporting copy. It is becoming the context layer of the post.

## Visuals attract attention. Captions create meaning.

A photograph can show us what something looks like. It cannot always tell us what it means.

A picture of a sneaker might document a new release, an archival discovery, a styling idea, a personal memory or a cultural reference. The pixels may look similar, but the story changes completely.

The caption tells us which story we are looking at.

That distinction matters on a platform where content increasingly travels beyond the people who already follow an account. A post might appear through recommendations, Instagram search, Google or a private share from someone who understands the reference but knows the recipient might not.

The further content travels from its original community, the more context it needs.

That makes the caption responsible for three different jobs.

It helps the existing community understand the creator’s point of view. It gives a new audience enough information to enter the conversation. And it provides Instagram and search engines with clearer signals about what the content represents.

The visual earns the pause. The caption makes the pause worthwhile.

## This does not mean longer is better

Instagram chief Adam Mosseri has previously said that [longer captions do not automatically increase reach](https://wersm.com/adam-mosseri-longer-captions-wont-increase-reach/).

There is no real contradiction here.

Caption length is a format choice. Context is a strategic requirement.

A concise caption can be descriptive, distinctive and useful. A long caption can still say very little. Adding 300 words of generic storytelling will not rescue an idea that lacks relevance, just as stuffing a caption with keywords will not make it valuable to an audience.

The goal is not to write more. The goal is to make every word perform a function.

A useful caption should answer at least one question the visual cannot:

Why does this matter? What should the audience notice? What does the brand believe? Why is this worth saving, sharing or discussing?

If it only describes what people can already see, it is probably not adding enough.

## Captions are becoming part of search strategy

Instagram has advised creators to place relevant keywords in captions for years because its search system uses text to understand and retrieve content.

That role has expanded. Public content from eligible professional accounts can also be [indexed by external search engines](https://help.instagram.com/147542625391305/), turning Instagram posts into part of the searchable web.

A caption can therefore influence how a post is understood inside Instagram and how it is discovered outside the app.

This does not mean captions should read like badly optimized webpages.

Searchable language should still sound human. The best keywords are often simply the clear, specific words people naturally use when talking about the subject.

For brands, this requires closer collaboration between creative, community and search teams. The caption cannot be the final task handed to a social media manager five minutes before publishing. It needs to be considered while the idea is being developed.

What should someone feel when they see the post? What should they understand after reading it? What language would they use to find it again?

Those are creative questions as much as SEO questions.

## Context becomes more valuable as content becomes abundant

Generative tools are making it easier to produce polished images, videos and variations at extraordinary speed.

That abundance makes visual quality less differentiating on its own.

Point of view, cultural understanding and editorial judgment become more valuable because they explain why a particular image deserves to exist.

The caption is one of the few places where a brand can turn an attractive asset into an identifiable perspective.

It can provide provenance. It can credit a collaborator. It can acknowledge a reference. It can explain why a moment matters to a particular community. It can give an audience language they want to repeat.

That is the strategic opportunity Instagram’s practical advice points toward.

Captions are not simply text placed beneath the content.

They are part of the content architecture.

The visual may stop the scroll. But the caption gives people a reason to care, a way to find the post and something meaningful to carry into the next conversation.

In a searchable social web, understanding is becoming distribution.

kept.heading: BRANDS ARE PAYING TO GET INTO AI ANSWERS. PUBLISHERS ARE DELETING THE PAGES THAT PUT THEM THERE (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: As search traffic declines, publishers are removing sponsored articles from their archives and charging brands to restore them. This creates a new risk for paid content, especially as those pages can also influence AI search visibility. Brands should negotiate retention terms upfront and regularly audit placements to catch removals early. Dated snapshots can also provide evidence if content disappears.
kept.article_text:
Title: Brands Are Paying to Get Into AI Answers. Publishers Are Deleting the Pages That Put Them There.

URL Source: https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/advertorial-takedown-restore-fees

Published Time: 2026-08-24T02:53:14.131Z

Markdown Content:
The email usually lands four to eight months after the campaign closed. It is polite and administrative in tone. Following an editorial review, the sponsored piece has been removed from the site. If the brand would like it restored, here is the rate.

Nothing in that message is illegal. In most cases nothing in it even breaks a contract, because there is rarely a clause covering how long the piece stays up. Advertorial has run for fifteen years on a shared assumption that published meant permanent. Almost nobody put that assumption in writing.

## The traffic math stopped working and the ad business went with it

Publishers did not wake up greedy. They woke up short.

Chartbeat data given exclusively to Axios in March showed [search referral traffic down 60 percent for small publishers over two years](https://www.axios.com/2026/03/17/chartbeat-search-traffic-ai-chatbots), 47 percent for mid-sized ones and 22 percent for the largest. The same dataset put Google referrals across more than 2,500 news sites [down 34 percent between December 2024 and December 2025](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/31/google-search-publishers-seo-geo-llms-ai). SparkToro's read of Similarweb numbers has [the zero-click rate at 68 percent in the first four months of 2026](https://news.designrush.com/ai-overviews-publisher-traffic-website-strategy-2026), up from 60 percent in 2024.

The money followed the audience out. Digiday reported in July that publisher ad request volumes in the second quarter [fell by roughly 32 to 37 percent year over year in the US and 39 to 41 percent in the UK](https://digiday.com/media/publisher-ad-supply-fell-by-up-to-40-in-q2-as-ai-search-choked-the-open-web/), measured across some 20 billion impressions. Advertising Week has [publishers reporting revenue declines of 50 to 90 percent](https://advertisingweek.com/the-search-traffic-collapse-is-forcing-publishers-to-adapt/) as referrals evaporate.

Branded content was supposed to be the hedge against exactly this. Digiday's 2026 survey of publisher revenue streams ranked it [second only to direct-sold advertising](https://digiday.com/media/digiday-research-how-dow-jones-forbes-the-guardian-and-other-publisher-revenue-streams-are-shifting-in-2026/), ahead of programmatic, events and video. When the second-biggest line on the P&L starts to wobble too, finance gets inventive. And the archive is the only inventory in the building that somebody has already paid for once.

## Four ways a placement dies, and only one of them looks deliberate

Practitioners who audit placements for a living describe a consistent set of failures. The link gets stripped while the article stays live. The link stays visible but quietly picks up a nofollow or sponsored attribute. The page gets deindexed while still loading normally for anyone who visits it. Or the page goes altogether, sometimes redirecting to the homepage so that nothing obviously breaks. The link-buying marketplace Serpverse [lays out the taxonomy](https://serpverse.io/blog/guest-post-link-removed) in a guide aimed at buyers trying to work out what happened to placements they paid for.

From a reporting dashboard all four look the same. The placement simply stops working.

The causes are mixed, and most of them are boring. Sites change hands and the new owner purges anything that looks paid. A CMS migration mangles outbound links and nobody checks afterwards. An editor gets nervous about search policy and blanket-nofollows every external link on the domain. Serpverse also names the uncomfortable one, which is that the slot gets resold, and notes that a site running several sponsored pieces a week has the weakest possible incentive to maintain any single one of them.

What has changed is that the industry handed publishers a respectable vocabulary for doing it. Content pruning, defined by Search Engine Land as [removing, consolidating, redirecting or deindexing pages](https://searchengineland.com/guide/content-pruning) that no longer earn their place, is now standard practice and standard advice. It is also a perfect cover story. Any takedown can be described as a quality decision, and the resale never has to come up.

Google has been noticeably unenthusiastic about the aggressive version. After CNET [deleted thousands of archive pages](https://buzzsumo.com/blog/content-pruning/), the company's Search Liaison [pushed back publicly](https://shortlist.io/blog/seo-content-pruning/), saying that deleting content because you think Google dislikes old content is not something its guidance encourages. The practice spread anyway. It solves a publisher problem that has very little to do with rankings.

## Almost nobody catches it in time

This works because the buy side is not looking. Removals are found by accident, months late, during an unrelated audit or when rankings drift and somebody goes hunting for a reason.

By then there is nothing left to push against. A placement arranged over email with no written terms has no retention clause to enforce, so there is no agreement to point at. Marketplaces often treat the order as closed the moment the piece goes live, which makes a removal four weeks later the buyer's problem rather than the publisher's. A chargeback is the wrong tool as well, since the placement was in fact delivered.

That leaves the brand choosing between writing off the original spend or paying a second time for something it thought it owned. Enough of them pay. Which is why the tactic keeps spreading.

## The stakes went up for a reason nobody has priced in

The archive has quietly become retrieval corpus as well as a traffic asset.

Every major AI search product pulls live pages and builds answers from them, which means [the quality of AI answers depends directly on the health of the underlying content layer](https://pro.edgex.exchange/en-US/news/article/ai-search-reshapes-web-traffic). A sponsored page that gets deindexed does not just stop passing authority to your site. It stops being available as a source to the systems that increasingly decide how your category gets described to buyers.

Brands have spent eighteen months trying to buy their way into AI citations. Quietly losing the pages they already paid for is a strange way to run that strategy, and most of them have no idea it is happening.

## What the takedown email actually tells you

Read it as information rather than as an insult, because it is unusually clear information.

A publisher that starts monetising its archive instead of its audience has stopped selling access and started liquidating. That approach works once per advertiser. It also prices in the assumption that the relationship has no future, which is the kind of assumption that makes itself true.

It tells you something about what you bought, too. Not a placement so much as a tenancy, with no lease, terminable at will, on land the landlord has begun selling off in pieces.

The fixes are unglamorous and mostly contractual. Get the retention term in writing before the money moves; a publisher who will not answer the question of how long the piece stays up has told you a lot. Audit placements quarterly rather than annually, because a removal caught inside a month is usually recoverable and one caught inside a year usually is not. Take a dated snapshot at publication, which turns an accusation into evidence. Weight spend toward outlets that run a handful of sponsored pieces a year over ones that run several a week.

The bigger correction is the one this publication keeps running into from different angles. Rented distribution is repricing in real time and the repricing is not finished. Owned media is not a cure for that, and plenty of brand newsrooms will fail on their own merits. But it has one property a purchased advertorial does not. Nobody can send you an invoice to put it back.

**Editor's note:** the takedown-and-restore pattern described here is drawn from buy-side accounts across several categories. Publishers named above are cited for industry data only, and no allegation is made that any of them engages in the practice.

kept.heading: AUTO-TRANSLATE WON'T WIN EU SHOPPERS (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Auto translation can make an ecommerce site readable, but human localization is needed to make it credible and convert shoppers. CSA Research found that 40% of consumers would not buy from a website in a foreign language, while only 20% of Germans and 13% of Poles bought from sellers in other EU countries in 2024. Brands should start with one or two high potential markets, localize product and transactional content, and use native speakers to review sales critical pages, checkout, returns, and emails. Track conversion, search traffic, and engagement by market to identify localization gaps and decide where to expand.
kept.article_text:
Title: Auto-Translate Won’t Win E.U. Shoppers

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/auto-translate-wont-win-e-u-shoppers

Published Time: 2026-08-25T14:19:28+00:00

Markdown Content:
In 2021 CSA Research, a Massachusetts-based consultancy, [surveyed](https://insights.csa-research.com/aim/en/reports/305013270/marketing) 9,909 consumers in 33 countries. Forty percent of respondents said they would not buy from a website in a foreign language.

Localization for merchants can seem as simple as turning on an ecommerce platform’s automatic translation. But readable is not the same as credible.

I’m writing this from my native Poland. In E.U. markets, where shoppers are already wary of cross-border sellers, auto-translation is only the first step.

![Image 1: Photo of global citizens holding their country flag](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/European-citizens-570x255.jpg)

Nearly all Europeans have used the internet. Roughly three-quarters of those have purchased goods online.

### Trust

Eurostat, the statistical office of the E.U., found in 2025 that 95% of European adults had used the internet and 78% of those had purchased online ([PDF](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/SEPDF/cache/46776.pdf)).

The shoppers are there.

Yet _cross-border_ buying remains relatively low in some markets. Only 20% of Germans and 13% of Poles bought from sellers in other E.U. countries in 2024, according to a report from Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences. The cause is more than language: delivery, payments, price, returns, and trust matter too.

But language is arguably the [top hurdle](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/the-top-conversion-barrier-in-the-e-u). For many shoppers, awkward, overly literal copy is a warning. Machine translation gets the meaning but often stumbles on tone. The phrasing can be technically correct and still feel foreign, eroding trust before checkout.

Sometimes the best translation is an adaptation. A U.S. fashion store might describe an outerwear item as “your new go-to jacket.” A literal German version — “Ihre neue Jacke, zu der Sie immer greifen” — is understandable but off. A local copywriter might choose “Ihre neue Lieblingsjacke für jeden Tag” (“your new favorite everyday jacket”).

It’s the same promise with a recognizable idiom.

### Engines

Translation software has improved, but I know of no universal solution. [DeepL](https://www.deepl.com/) offers glossaries and formal or informal tone controls and focuses on a smaller language set. [Google Cloud Translation](https://cloud.google.com/translate) includes more languages and publishes usage-based pricing.

Coverage, features, and prices change continually; compare platforms in real time rather than rely on a fixed, dated ranking. Test on your own product pages, support copy, and checkout before choosing.

I admit an affinity for DeepL: its founder is a fellow Pole. In my experience, DeepL’s European-language output is more natural, but results vary by language pair, content type, terminology, and brand voice.

And nothing replaces a human review. Software can narrow the gap, but it doesn’t remove accountability.

French copy often uses a formal form of address; a German store must choose between du and Sie. French copy written for France may not fit Belgium. German copy may require different shipping, tax, payment, and address information for Germany than for Austria.

Currency, prices, dates, measurements, address fields, payment options, and transactional messages also need local treatment. An otherwise localized product page can feel unfinished when reviews and FAQs remain in English.

### Search

Search engine optimization for multiple languages is rare. Google introduced the [_hreflang_ HTML attribute](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/hreflang-explained) in 2011 to help it and other search engines detect local languages. Yet only about 20% of global websites use _hreflang,_ per published reports.

Machine translation doesn’t violate Google’s rules and can still rank. The SEO risk comes from publishing thousands of unreviewed, near-duplicate translations merely to capture traffic.

### Start Small

Don’t attempt to translate an ecommerce site into every E.U. language. Choose one or two markets based on demand, margins, and existing traffic. Create a glossary for product names and brand terminology and use a storefront localization app for the first pass. [Weglot](https://www.weglot.com/) is cross-platform and runs on DeepL, Google, and others. Shopify’s free [Translate & Adapt](https://apps.shopify.com/translate-and-adapt) is enough to test a market or two. WooCommerce stores can use [WPML](https://wpml.org/).

Retain a native-language specialist to review the pages that drive sales, such as product descriptions, checkout, returns, and transactional emails.

Then track conversion rates, search traffic, and customer engagement by market. The results will show what needs improving and where to expand next.

kept.heading: COPYWRITING FRIDAY: DUMB WAYS TO DIE (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The “Dumb Ways to Die” campaign shows that unwelcome messages can perform better when audiences are given a reason to engage before receiving the actual ask. Metro Trains Melbourne turned a safety warning into an entertaining music video that reached more than 340 million people, then delivered the safety message only at the end. Marketers can apply the same approach by leading with delight, using memorable rhymes, and replacing abstract claims with vivid, specific details that create mental images. The broader lesson is to make people want to consume the message instead of simply making an unwanted message louder.
kept.article_text:
Title: Copywriting Friday: Dumb Ways to Die

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/dumb-ways-to-die-copywriting-friday/

Published Time: 2026-08-18

Markdown Content:
[Copywriting Friday](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#copywriting-friday) highlights the tools and techniques of persuasive content. Some of the examples may seem dated, but the principles are timeless (and critical for conversion rate optimization). Enjoy.

Most businesses, at some point, need to communicate things that their audience would really prefer not to bother with. A website cookie message, a compliance disclaimer, a terms and conditions checkbox.

That’s not to say that these things aren’t important. They can be very important, but that doesn’t stop them **draining a visitor’s attention or interest**. The usual fix is to say the boring but important message louder, or in such a way that visitors are forced to interact.

But there is an alternative worth considering.

## 340 million spoonfuls of sugar

**Instead of shouting louder, you make the message something people might actually want to consume and even share.** Mary Poppins called this strategy “a spoonful of sugar,” and in this Copywriting Friday, we’re going to look at one of the most extreme examples of it that we’ve ever come across.

In November 2012, **Metro Trains Melbourne and their agency McCann released a train‑safety film that more than 340 million people chose to watch**. It became the most‑awarded campaign in the 60‑year history of the Cannes Lions, taking a record five Grand Prix. And it did that by refusing to be a safety message at all, until the final few seconds.

Here’s the video, but fair warning. This is a tune that can get stuck in your head.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJNR2EpS0jw)

Metro Trains Melbourne, “Dumb Ways to Die” (2012).

The song opens with no trains in sight, just a cheerful little band finding inventive ways to end themselves:

> Set fire to your hair.
> 
> Poke a stick at a grizzly bear.
> 
> Eat medicine that’s out of date.
> 
> Use your private parts as piranha bait.

Then the chorus, the part you will be humming an hour from now:

> Dumb ways to die.
> 
> So many dumb ways to die.

If you watch it through once, there’s a high chance that you’ll be compromised. That is the whole trick, so let’s break it into pieces you can actually use.

## Change the medium, not just how you say it

Most safety campaigns try to word the warning better. McCann started somewhere else. Their executive creative director, John Mescall, put the problem in a sentence:

> The aim of this campaign is to engage an audience that really doesn’t want to hear any kind of safety message, and we think dumb ways to die will.

In other words, the goal was not a clearer warning. It was attention from people who wouldn’t normally give any.

**So the team changed what the thing _was_, from a public-service announcement to a music video… and later a mobile game that hit number one in 22 countries.**

Of course, not everyone has the budget or need to go this far. What matters more is the mindset. _How can I make my message more engaging for my audience?_ (That’s the kind of question that inspired us to write about [Better Call Saul](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/better-call-cro-why-breaking-bads-saul-goodman-is-a-conversion-rate-genius/) or [Any Given Sunday](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/a-game-of-inches-copywriting-friday/).)

What is your version of the safety warning, the disclaimer nobody reads, or the funnel page that people bounce from? And more importantly… **what would make someone actually want to reach the end of it?** The mindset isn’t just for “boring” pages; it can apply anywhere.

For example, the playful design and copy of [PostHog’s website](https://posthog.com/).

![Image 1: Screenshot of PostHog’s playful, illustrated homepage aimed at app developers.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/post-hog.jpg)

If you are in PostHog’s target market of app developers, you’ll likely be delighted by their website long before you get to buy anything.

But wait, we’re getting ahead of ourselves…

## Lead with the delight

**For almost the whole song, there is no train safety anywhere**, only cute characters eating out-of-date medicine and offering themselves to piranhas. The real message arrives in the closing verse, and the song winks as it makes the switch:

> Stand on the edge of a train station platform. Drive around the boom gates at a level crossing. Run across the tracks between the platforms. They may not rhyme, but they’re quite possibly the dumbest ways to die.

By the time you reach train tracks, you are already invested. You have laughed (or at least smiled) at the inanity of the video, and you have caught the chorus. **When the “ask” finally comes, you are a receptive audience instead of a defensive one.**

![Image 2: Still from the “Dumb Ways to Die” video showing one of the bean characters standing on the edge of a train platform during the closing safety verse.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/train-crossing-dumb-ways-to-die.jpg)

This is related to Joe Sugarman’s [slippery slide](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/conversion-funnel/). In the classic book, _The Adweek Copywriting Handbook_, he argued that the only job of your headline is to get the reader to read the first line, whose only job is to get them to the second, and so on. **Each element carries the reader on so smoothly that stopping feels like more effort than continuing.**

Now look at your own funnel. Is there anywhere that you are _serving the vegetables first_? As important as they are, these places are potential leaks in your funnel. Is there anything you can do to **earn your visitors’ patience before you spend it**?

## Give your audience some rhyme time

There is a reason that many people are still singing Dumb Ways to Die hours or days after they’ve seen it. In 2000, psychologists Matthew McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh [showed experimental participants real rhyming aphorisms next to reworded versions](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11228916/). For example:

> What sobriety conceals, alcohol reveals.

Became:

> What sobriety conceals, alcohol unmasks.

Would it surprise you to know that the _participants rated the rhyming versions as more accurate descriptions of human behavior_, even though the claims were identical? That’s because the **rhyme is easier to process, and we quietly mistake that mental fluency for truth**. This is the [rhyme-as-reason effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyme-as-reason_effect).

Of course, you need not be a composer to use it. Marketers have mined this for decades, from Pringles’ “Once you pop, you can’t stop” to Folgers’ “The best part of wakin’ up is Folgers in your cup.”

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ers_9vyg3_4)

Backed with the right research, rhymes can work almost anywhere, including product names, headlines, email subjects and more. Find an opportunity and A/B test it out.

As we have said repeatedly over the past twenty years… **companies that test, grow to be best**.

(You get the idea.)

## Absurd specificity makes mental movies

“Be careful around trains” is forgettable because it is abstract; there is nothing to picture. “Use your private parts as piranha bait” is unforgettable because it is absurdly and painfully concrete.

![Image 3: Still from the “Dumb Ways to Die” video showing a bean character using itself as piranha bait, the absurdly specific image from the opening verse.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/pirana-bait-dumb-ways-to-die.jpg)

You can see it, however much you would rather not. **Every dumb death in the song is a tiny, vivid, particular image, not a general caution.**

This is a rule we come back to constantly [in this series](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#copywriting-friday). **Concrete and specific beats the generic, every time.** A specific detail plays a mental movie; an abstraction plays nothing.

Find the abstraction in your own copy. Where are you writing “trusted by many businesses” when you could write the one specific, verifiable, pictureable detail that a reader would struggle to forget?

## The real lesson

The instinct with an unwelcome message is to keep polishing the warning until it finally lands. “Dumb Ways to Die” suggests the opposite.

**Do not say the avoided thing better. Earn the right to say it at all** by making something people genuinely want, and _letting your real message ride in on its back_.

The final safety lines in the song do not rhyme because they did not need to. By the time they land, the audience is already singing.
