Title: Has Google demoted listicles?

URL Source: https://www.growth-memo.com/p/has-google-demoted-listicles

Published Time: 2026-08-24T19:18:49+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_T-u!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7d225d90-b7b2-4716-9bf2-09cbb9320d66_1672x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_T-u!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7d225d90-b7b2-4716-9bf2-09cbb9320d66_1672x941.png)

This Memo was sent to 28,869 subscribers. Welcome to +70 new readers! Sign up for free to get new insights every week, or sign up for Premium to get exclusive tools and frameworks that make you more effective.

Aren’t listicles dead? Brands have been writing self-serving listicles as a classic SEO play for years, and many have ramped up production at the start of AI Search due to their outsized influence on citations. But over the last 12 months, we’ve seen growing evidence that the tactic of editorial “best of” or roundup pages has run its course.

Lots of great research over the last 12 months from experts like [Lily Ray](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/is-google-finally-cracking-down-on), [Nick Haigler](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/the-listicle-window-is-closing-in-ai-search-30-decline-mom), or [Glen Allsopp](https://ahrefs.com/blog/best-lists-research/)has shown that:

*   Listicles are the most-cited page type in ChatGPT answers at 43.8% of 26,283 source URLs, including lists where brands rank themselves first

*   Google began demoting sites built on self-serving listicles in January 2026, with several SaaS brands losing 29 to 49% of organic visibility within weeks

*   ChatGPT cut listicle citations by 30% from December 2025 to January 2026, with Wikipedia and Reddit absorbing the lost share

And yet, whenever I still use Google (which is not that often anymore), I still encounter listicles all the time. So, what gives? A few questions came up for me:

1.   How often are listicles still present?

2.   Can we spot a demotion of self-serving listicles?

3.   What are characteristics of a listicle that consistently performs well?

4.   Should companies write listicles at all?

I set out to find the answers to those questions with a large data pull: I analyzed 60,000 US-English desktop Google queries across 15 verticals using[SE Ranking](https://seranking.com/). The dataset contains 5.32 million organic-result rows collected during a 47-hour window in August 2026.

I’ll split the findings into two Memos: Memo one (this one) answers questions 1 and 2. Memo two (next week) will answer 3 and 4, so stay tuned.

A lot of confusion comes from not using the terminology correctly (tell me you’re a nerd without telling me you’re a nerd).

The word _listicle_ is a combination of _article_ and _list_. Or, in other words, a listicle is an article where the list is the content. The body consists of discrete, same-type items (tools, ideas, examples, options) that are comparable with each other. Each item gets a self-contained treatment (usually its own heading). And the title promises a bounded set, with or without a number in it.

A step-by-step tutorial (”How to set up Asana”) is sequential, not a listicle, because item 3 depends on item 2. Listicle items can be reordered without breaking the logic.

A few examples of listicles:

*   [https://www.nerdwallet.com/credit-cards/best/cash-back](https://www.nerdwallet.com/credit-cards/best/cash-back)

*   [https://www.tomshardware.com/reviews/best-gpus,4380.html](https://www.tomshardware.com/reviews/best-gpus,4380.html)

*   [https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/five-investing-ideas](https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/five-investing-ideas)

*   [https://www.salesforce.com/small-business/types-of-businesses/](https://www.salesforce.com/small-business/types-of-businesses/)

*   [https://travel.usnews.com/hotels/best-all-inclusive-resorts-in-usa/](https://travel.usnews.com/hotels/best-all-inclusive-resorts-in-usa/)

*   [https://www.healthline.com/health/fitness-exercise/at-home-workouts](https://www.healthline.com/health/fitness-exercise/at-home-workouts)

Listicles can come from different types of companies with varying incentives: affiliates like NerdWallet, publishers like US News, or brands like Salesforce.

*   **Website owner type**: brand, publisher, retailer, platform, nonprofit, or community

*   **Incentive:** self-promotional, affiliate-supported, independent, or unclear

60K US-English desktop Google queries were analyzed across 15 verticals using[SE Ranking data](https://seranking.com/).

This dataset contains 5.32M organic-result rows from a 47-hour window in August 2026.

Queries were stratified by vertical, query wording, and query length, then weighted to the intended sample mix.

*   Duplicate records and successful-but-empty SERPs were excluded.

*   A nested 20,000-query subset captured additional search-result features, including AI Overviews, video, images, People Also Ask, Reddit, and YouTube.

Each result was automatically classified as a listicle or not using its title, snippet, URL, and website type. The classification separated numbered list articles from unnumbered editorial roundups and excluded product grids, directories, forums, video pages, single-item reviews, and step-by-step guides.

The data pipeline was checked for completeness, duplicate queries, and rank integrity. I also manually reviewed website ownership and conducted a blind quality review of 30 pages. The initial classifier pilot achieved 100% precision and recall on 30 queries, but an untouched production holdout remains the final validation step.

The study is observational and reflects one crawl wave. It identifies associations between query wording, listicle presence, and ranking, not causal effects.

The results from this dataset do not show a universal penalty for listicles. At least one listicle appeared in the top 10 for 55.1% of queries and in the top three for 32.3%.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!n1YA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8212881d-42c7-449c-b2a1-52c7dfc31986_1680x1824.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!n1YA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8212881d-42c7-449c-b2a1-52c7dfc31986_1680x1824.png)

85.9% of search results pages contained at least one title with a broad list cue: a one-to-three-digit number or a word such as “best,” “top,” “ways,” “ideas,” “examples,” “alternatives,” “tips,” “tools,” “apps,” or “options.”

However, stronger classification shows a confirmed listicle on 55.1% of search results pages. In other words, **half of search results contain true listicles**.

The query itself is the biggest factor deciding whether Google shows a listicle or not. **Google shows 4.5x more listicles when users ask for a set of options.**

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ukzN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0c395545-ca80-45c4-81cf-ecd3697e15ae_1680x1824.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ukzN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0c395545-ca80-45c4-81cf-ecd3697e15ae_1680x1824.png)

*   When a query explicitly asks for ideas, examples, options, or the best items, listicles dominate the top results.

*   When the request for multiple options is only implied in a query, the listicle advantage largely disappears.

*   The top-three rate rose to 54.5% for explicit-list queries compared with 10.2% for implicit category or comparison queries.

*   The rate of listicle appearance was 12.1% for the comparison group of informational queries that did not ask for a list.

However, one suggestive hint that Google is demoting (self-serving) listicles is that almost half of them come from publishers _instead_ of known brands/vendors.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a2s2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6099867-e20f-4f2c-bc13-7293f65783f7_1680x1863.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a2s2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6099867-e20f-4f2c-bc13-7293f65783f7_1680x1863.png)

Publishers also won 54.0% of 4,026 direct matchups against a brand or vendor listicle on the same search results page. When examining the top 5 results in the SERP, the publisher averaged position 4.24 in those matchups, compared with 4.71 for the brand or vendor.

*   Publishing and content platforms had the strongest conditional rank at 3.76 when one of their listicles appeared in the top 10.

*   Publishers averaged 3.99, government, academic, and nonprofit sites averaged 4.48, and brands or vendors averaged 4.65.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UJY1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F29f38cf3-21d9-4aa5-90a3-2aaaf432e9e9_1620x2256.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UJY1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F29f38cf3-21d9-4aa5-90a3-2aaaf432e9e9_1620x2256.png)

The 5,765 domains that supplied top-10 listicle leaders point to a broad market with a long tail:

*   The top 10 domains accounted for 18.3%, and the top 50 accounted for 36.5%.

*   The remaining 5,715 domains accounted for 63.5%.

If a finding from this week changes a decision for your brand, the Growth Memo Premium Resource Library has 45+ (and growing) checklists, light tools, AI workflows, and stakeholder slide decks to put it to work. Switch to [Growth Premium](https://www.growth-memo.com/subscribe).

Self-promoting listicles come from brands (software companies, banks, service providers, etc.) that put themselves first in their lists to influence AI answers. A classic example is to write about the “x best [insert category]” and list yourself at the top. By the way, sometimes you can influence “objective” listicles (from affiliates or publishers) by paying for it, but Google cannot detect that since those transactions happen behind closed doors.

So now that we know that there is a difference between publishers who create listicles for products vs. self-serving listicles that come from brands, the question is whether the latter has seen a demotion since brands go bonkers with it?

We know from Lily Ray’s analyses that the unannounced mid-January Google update impacts listicles. I’ve observed the same, anecdotally. We also know from [Peec](https://peec.ai/blog/self-promotional-listicles-analysis-from-232k-citations)that there doesn’t seem to be a demotion for self-promoting listicles in citations across ChatGPT, Google AI, Perplexity, Copilot, Gemini, and AI Overviews.

In this study, I compared a fixed subset of 2,400 queries and 24,000 search results between January and August. The results: The search results changed substantially. Only 52.5% of queries had the same exact URL at position one in both periods, and only 58.3% had the same domain. **At position one, the conservative listicle range fell from 18.9% to 20.2% in January to 15.1% to 15.6% in August. Across the top three, the January range was 35.9% to 39.0%, compared with 32.0% to 33.0% in August.**

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2uwl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b6d6dbd-6d01-452a-827a-374f8d465081_1680x1890.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2uwl!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2b6d6dbd-6d01-452a-827a-374f8d465081_1680x1890.png)

That is the listicle penalty we’ve seen anecdotally. But I cannot trace it back to self-promoting listicles specifically. As a matter of fact, 62% of vendor-authored listicles gained estimated organic traffic since January, and the median page gained 38%.

Listicle occurrence in the organic top 10 ranged from 42.0% in entertainment and gaming to 67.2% in beauty and fashion. **B2B software reached 62.5%**, while travel reached 49.3%.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JdSB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F58de2e48-bcc7-4bd8-a7c2-dffd5a774e02_1475x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JdSB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F58de2e48-bcc7-4bd8-a7c2-dffd5a774e02_1475x2048.png)

Brand or vendor listicles varied even more. They appeared in the top 10 on 46.2% of B2B software search results pages, compared with 3.3% in food and 6.2% in travel.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!07Wo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c956c8d-1341-4d5e-96d6-4c905117c1c7_1530x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!07Wo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c956c8d-1341-4d5e-96d6-4c905117c1c7_1530x2048.png)

That, to me, is symptomatic of how B2B companies use listicles to “optimize” for AI Search, which is a much smaller lever for consumer-oriented verticals. After all, I’d argue it’s mostly B2B brands using listicles for AI Search optimization. However, it also shows that listicles are by no means dead.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4_es!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40806d3d-c7cd-49d5-a8f2-713f2599dd79_1203x698.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4_es!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40806d3d-c7cd-49d5-a8f2-713f2599dd79_1203x698.png)

Why do B2B teams pile into this tactic at all? Today’s sponsor has the demand-side data. For the [2026 Marketing Leaders Reality Index](https://realityindex.airops.com/?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=GLOBAL_en_CMO-Survey_Q3-2026), AirOps asked 300+ marketing execs what is actually happening inside their teams right now, not the polished version that shows up on LinkedIn:

*   86.6% are prioritizing AI search

*   75.4% got higher pipeline or revenue targets, but only 43.0% saw any budget increase

*   Only 23% feel confident measuring it

Read that against the numbers above: Everyone is told to win AI search, few get more resources, and almost nobody can prove impact. That’s the environment where cheap, scalable tactics like self-serving listicles thrive.

[Read the full report](https://realityindex.airops.com/?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=GLOBAL_en_CMO-Survey_Q3-2026)

Demotion or not, the reality is that listicles face heavy competition for attention. **92% of SERPs with a top-10 listicle also contained Reddit or YouTube somewhere on the page.** Both platforms appeared together on 53% of those SERPs.

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h2a4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4700fd8a-d53a-4bba-8aab-1fd197e4de09_1680x1824.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h2a4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4700fd8a-d53a-4bba-8aab-1fd197e4de09_1680x1824.png)

The practical consequence is that a page can lose attention (think: clicks) without losing its position among standard unpaid results. Listicle-related keywords seem like they carry high buyer intent, but don’t expect a flood of conversions amidst AI Overviews, Reddit, and Youtube. The average share of AI Overviews across all verticals was 83.7% to 93.4% in B2B, where listicles appear most!

Reddit and YouTube occupy different positions in the organic results.

*   Reddit placed in the top 3 on 70.7% of the search results pages where it appeared in the top 10. YouTube did so on 11.1%.

*   When Reddit appeared in the top 10, its best result averaged position 3.31 and had a median position of 2. YouTube averaged position 6.62 and had a median position of 7.

*   Reddit and YouTube can appear as ordinary links, embedded result boxes, and sources in Google’s AI-generated answer for the same query.

*   Reddit ranked above YouTube on 84.5% of the 19,729 search results pages where both appeared in the top 10. The Reddit advantage reached 90.4% on explicit list queries and fell to 69.9% on implicit category or comparison queries.

*   YouTube gains more reach outside ordinary organic results. In the 20K-query advanced panel, video boxes and AI Overview citations added 20.7 percentage points of YouTube reach beyond search results pages where YouTube already ranked in the organic top 10. The same increase for Reddit was 2.1 percentage points.

The next budget review will ask why organic search optimization spend matters when Reddit, YouTube, and AI Overviews take the click. Get [Growth Premium](https://www.growth-memo.com/subscribe).

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6LzC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe53cbc6-fcdf-4c31-bbf8-87923137d350_1503x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6LzC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe53cbc6-fcdf-4c31-bbf8-87923137d350_1503x2048.png)

The platform pattern also changes by vertical.

*   Reddit had greater organic top-10 presence than YouTube in 11 of 15 verticals. Its largest advantages appeared in travel (+40.6 percentage points), education and careers (+22.8), finance (+21.9), family and pets (+21.1), and automotive (+19.6).

*   YouTube led in 4 verticals: food (+40.8 percentage points), health (+19.1), home and DIY (+15.1), and beauty and fashion (+6.1).

*   Reddit’s organic top-10 presence peaked at 77.1% in automotive and fell to 25.7% in health.

*   YouTube peaked at 78.1% in food and fell to 29.7% in travel.

The pattern suggests different platform roles. Reddit is stronger in research and comparison-oriented categories, while YouTube is stronger where visual demonstration, inspiration, or instruction matters.

**Has Google demoted listicles? Yes, In a very targeted way.** We see almost 4% fewer listicles in position 1 and the top 3. And yet, they remain very present in Google’s search results. Listicles that are performing well in August have even gained traffic since January. So, Google has systematically and carefully weeded out certain listicles.

My take is that the aggressive use of AI to create (poor) listicles has led to a flood that Google targeted with the secret mid-January update. Quality and velocity seem to be markers in Google’s latest spam algorithm updates.

That said, and this is the bigger issue here: Even where listicles perform well, the click opportunity shrinks. 92% of listicle SERPs carry Reddit or YouTube results; 93.4% of listicle-related B2B query results have AI Overviews.

Look, I have my own moral judgments about self-promoting listicles. There’s a degree of cringe to it. There is also a degree of business impact to it, though we don’t know how much. So, the way I reconcile the two is by seeking evidence for putting yourself first. For example, can your G2 grid position or reviews support that “you’re the best”?

Next week, we’ll dive deep into my observations on what well-performing listicles do better than others, and whether it’s still worth creating listicles.

Humbly,

Kevin

*   Display ad industry metrics include average click-through rate, average cost per click, and average cost per lead.
*   High-impact, video, and native display ads metrics include click-through rate, video completion rate, and viewability.

The metrics we chose to look at are specific to the nature of display ads. Display ads impact conversion rates indirectly (which is a measurement called view-through conversions), but they naturally have lower conversion rates attached to them directly, which is why we decided to omit that metric.

“My biggest advice when evaluating visual ad formats is to honor that they might not be delivering conversions themselves. Even when they do, they should not be held to the same benchmarks as search formats,” said Navah Hopkins, Ad Product Liaison at Microsoft.

Meanwhile, display ads yield tons of impressions, so even though their click-through rates look quite low if you compare them to other tactics like search ads, that can still equate to a lot of impactful clicks in the grand scheme of impressions versus clicks.

“Most people aren’t going to immediately click a display ad. They’ll come back to your site directly, weeks or months later, when they need you,” said Greg Carter, Vice President of Marketing at [Clutch](https://clutch.co/).

Ultimately, you want your display ads to get seen (or watched) and turn into real results, which is why we included viewability, video completion rate, cost per click, and cost per lead.

## Tips for the best display ads

Whether you’re new to display advertising or a seasoned display campaign veteran, this benchmark data can be a practical reference point when assessing and optimizing your strategy.

“I read these benchmarks as targets. I want to be above the number for my industry,” Greg said.

Ready to take your display and video ads to the next level? Here are some display advertising tips (based on this data) to help you get started.

### 1. Try a variety of placements

On average, all of the display ad types we covered in this report brought in a good number of clicks and views. For maximum reach, be sure to have display ad creative that’s flexible across major placements on the [Google Display Network](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/google-display-network) (including YouTube), Microsoft Audience Network, USA TODAY Network, and more.

“Display can add depth to your strategy—just simply getting in front of your target audience and reinforcing your position in their mind is deeply valuable,” said Brett McHale, Founder of [Empiric Marketing](https://empiricmarketing.com/).

![Image 15: display video ads benchmarks - placement examples](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/display-video-ads-benchmarks-placement-variety.webp)

### 2. Prioritize your display budgets when allocating ad spend

It can be easy to let your display campaigns fall by the wayside when[planning your budgets](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/google-ads-budget), but it’s not that search ads are better than display or vice versa; they’re complementary to one another. Your display ads are part of your [pre-marketing strategy](https://localiq.com/blog/influence-buyers-before-search/), meaning you want them to be familiar with your business before it’s even time to buy the types of products and services you offer. This drives users to search for your business later.

“What makes display advertising so useful is that it can be leveraged at the beginning of the customer journey to inspire awareness, just as easily as it can remind a customer to complete their transaction towards the end with remarketing,” Navah said.

So, while you can factor in that display ads have a lower average CPC than search ads, you’ll want to treat budget allocations similarly. With display ads, you’re often paying per view or impression, rather than per click. You’ll need a competitive budget to get seen as much as possible.

“One way to improve display performance is to have a larger budget allocated for these types of campaigns. More budget means more impressions, and more data to optimize with,” said Rhett Chassereau, Supervisor of Programmatic Buying & Optimization at USA TODAY Co.

### 3. Continuously test different creative elements

While you’ll want to leverage multiple placement types across networks in your display strategy, you should also constantly test various creative elements. For example, see if your audience is more receptive to certain color schemes, image types, calls to action, and more.

“Cycle in new creative and make multiple copy variations for each. Launch a number of ads and find out which one performs the best,” Brett said.

“From there, you can take the top-performing and make more variations of them,” he added.

Like anything with [PPC advertising](https://www.wordstream.com/ppc), testing your display ads will be a bit of a balancing act that requires both patience and agility.

“Give the channel time, then be proactive about your display ad creative. Judge individual ads fast and rotate them out as soon as the data is clear. But judge overall display campaigns more cautiously, because they’re a brand play that won’t necessarily pay back on a short timeline,” Greg said.

![Image 16: display video ads benchmarks - ab test example](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/display-video-ads-benchmarks-ab-tes-example-1.webp)

### 4. Use AI to scale your display ads

AI, when used thoughtfully, can help you quickly scale your display campaigns. For instance, it can help you brainstorm test ideas or quickly duplicate and tweak current creative your team has designed. Just be sure to give any AI-generated display assets a final, manual edit before you set them live to avoid any [glaring AI fails](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ai-fails) or off-brand elements.

## What these display and video ads benchmarks mean for your business

Whatever your industry, you can make display ads work for your business. Display ads help you reach a wide but highly qualified audience. You can remarket to potential customers already interested in your business and pre-market to brand-new potential customers, too. Just be ready to flex your display strategy according to test results and placement trends, so your display ads always catch the attention you’re looking to grab.

For more help making the most of your display ads, see how [our solutions](https://www.wordstream.com/marketing-services?cid=Web_WS_InContent_Demo_Blog_Demo) can maximize your campaign strategy!

All currency values are posted in USD.

Title: Which Marketing Metric Should You Actually Trust?

URL Source: https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/marketing-measurement-mmm-attribution-incrementality/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T13:10:32+00:00

Markdown Content:
Your platform numbers say a channel is delivering strong ROAS. Your MMM suggests you’ve probably overspent there. An incrementality test indicates a positive lift. Which number should determine where the next dollar goes?

The instinct is often to deem one of these as the ‘Source of Truth’, but in every likelihood all of these models are wrong to a certain degree. Each measurement method is giving you an answer, but most likely to different questions. The more useful approach is to start with the decision you’re trying to make, then establish which evidence should have the authority to make it.

## **Begin by giving each measurement method a job**

At Brainlabs, we think about measurement as a connected system with different methodologies operating at different levels. MMM informs strategic allocation, helping determine where investment should broadly move across the media mix. Incrementality validates causality, testing whether an intervention actually created an outcome that wouldn’t otherwise have happened. Attribution and platform signals support day-to-day, mostly in-channel, optimization, helping teams make faster decisions within those broader investment guardrails.

The same channel can look very different through each lens without one of them necessarily being wrong. A platform can be extremely good at identifying people likely to convert and therefore report strong returns, while an incrementality test reveals that many of those customers would have purchased anyway. Both findings are useful. They simply shouldn’t be allowed to make the same decision.

Once you establish those decision rights, the question changes from “Which number is right?” to “Which number is right for the decision I’m making?”

## **Don’t be afraid of measurement failure**

If MMM suggests a channel has significant headroom but an incrementality test finds limited causal impact, averaging the two results until they tell a more comfortable story won’t help. The discrepancy is telling you there’s something worth investigating. Perhaps the experimental window isn’t capturing longer-term effects. Perhaps the test design or audience introduces a limitation. Or perhaps an assumption in the MMM needs to be revisited.

The same applies when platform ROAS looks exceptional but incremental performance is weak. That gap can reveal something important about the role the channel is actually playing: it may be highly effective at finding and converting existing demand without creating as much additional demand as the attributed return suggests.

This is where multiple measurement methods become more valuable than one. Each can expose assumptions the others can’t see. Use measurement failure to identify where your understanding of performance needs to get sharper.

## **Make your measurement methods learn from each other**

The next step is making sure that insight doesn’t stay trapped inside whichever analysis produced it.

Suppose MMM identifies potential headroom in a channel. Rather than immediately making a large allocation change, that finding can become a hypothesis for experimentation. A controlled test establishes whether increasing spend genuinely creates incremental growth. That causal evidence can then feed back into future planning, strengthening or challenging the assumptions that informed the original recommendation.

The same loop should continue into execution. Strategic measurement establishes where investment should broadly go, experimentation pressure-tests the decisions that matter most, and attribution and platform signals help teams optimize within the resulting guardrails.

So rather than three competing versions of performance, you get a feedback loop:

MMM identifies the opportunity, experimentation tests the assumption, the learning improves future planning, attribution guides execution within those boundaries.

The value comes from the connection between them. Each methodology makes the next decision better informed.

## **Decide disagreements before they become political**

This becomes particularly important at enterprise scale, where different teams naturally gravitate toward different evidence. Performance teams have platform data, analytics teams may own MMM and experimentation, while finance has its own view of revenue and return. Without an agreed hierarchy, measurement disagreements can quickly become organizational ones.

The answer isn’t choosing one metric that everyone has to use. It’s agreeing upfront on which evidence governs which type of decision and what happens when signals conflict.

That means defining the rules before the numbers arrive. Which methodology determines strategic budget allocation? When should an incrementality test challenge an existing assumption? Which signals can teams use to optimize independently, and when does a decision become significant enough to require a different level of evidence?

This is what turns measurement from a collection of reports into a decision-making system. Teams can still look at different metrics because they have different jobs to do, but everyone understands how those metrics ultimately connect back to investment decisions.

## **Stop looking for one measurement truth**

Modern marketing is too complex for one methodology to answer every question well. Trying to force MMM, incrementality and attribution into agreement can remove the very differences that make having multiple methods useful in the first place.

Start with the decision. Give each methodology a clear job. When the evidence disagrees, investigate what the gap is telling you. Then feed what you learn back into the system so the next decision starts with better information than the last.

The goal isn’t to find the one number everyone can agree on.

It’s to know which number deserves to make the decision.

Title: SEO is the cleanup crew for organisational dysfunction

URL Source: https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T20:33:23+00:00

Markdown Content:
24th August, 2026

![Image 1](https://www.jonoalderson.com/wp-content/uploads/dysfunction-760x350.png)

When something breaks on the website, more often than not, it’s the SEO team that finds it. A redesign doubles page weight. Product pages inherit three teams’ worth of contradictory messaging. Analytics stops measuring the thing everyone presents to the board. Nobody has looked at what customers have been saying on Reddit for six months. Eventually, somebody notices. And it’s usually _us_.

This is partly a consequence of where SEO sits. We work across technology, content, brand, product, PR, analytics, and whichever other department has accidentally affected whether people can find, understand or trust the business this week. That makes SEO a[meta-discipline](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/from-meta-tags-to-meta-discipline/), not a tidy marketing channel in a tidy box on the org chart.

A technical audit exposes an engineering problem. Keyword research reveals that customers describe the category differently from the company. A visibility decline turns out to have very little to do with rankings; the business has become harder to recommend.

SEO inherits performance because nobody owns it, structured data because engineering finds it boring, and product copy because apparently somebody has to explain what the thing does.

There is satisfaction in walking into a mess and leaving it less broken. But an organisation with a reliable cleanup crew has less reason to stop making the mess. That’s the trap: a team rewarded for catching failures it has no authority to prevent. SEO keeps ending up here because of what it can see.

## [Why SEO keeps finding the bodies](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-why-seo-keeps-finding-the-bodies)

SEO is _nosy_. We crawl, compare and measure everything, then spend an unhealthy amount of time asking why one thing behaves differently from another. The website is only the start. We look at demand, competitors, reviews, citations, forums, performance data, analytics, and whatever machines make of the lot.

Most teams see their own system. Engineering sees the platform. Brand sees the message. Product sees the problem it solves. Support sees the customer in front of them. SEO sees some of the joins and what leaks through them.

That view is not unique to SEO. Good researchers, analysts and product teams also work across organisational boundaries. But SEO’s advantage is more prosaic: a large and rather strange collection of external signals routinely lands on our desks.

Once those signals are treated as evidence about the business, the limits of conventional SEO become obvious. That’s why [SEO is no longer enough](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/seo-is-no-longer-enough/), and why [SEO vs GEO is the wrong question](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/seo-vs-geo/). The interesting problem is whether the market can understand, evaluate and recommend the business. Search gives us one view of that, albeit a noisy and incomplete one.

Search demand exposes differences between the market’s language and the company’s internal model. Reviews show where the brand promise has wandered away from the customer experience. Crawl and performance data can reveal engineering debt. Content gaps may indicate missing expertise, weak ownership, or a product nobody quite knows how to explain.

These are clues, not diagnoses. Rankings, clicks, and citations are outputs from a larger system, which is one reason I’ve argued that [clicks don’t count](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/clicks-dont-count/). A dashboard is not an oracle simply because it contains several decimals.

One angry Reddit post proves very little. Several independent signals pointing at the same weakness deserve attention. The useful question is not just how to improve the metric, but what else might have produced it, and whether the organisation can prevent it happening again.

## [Capability gaps](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-capability-gaps)

When the same kind of problem keeps returning, the organisation is missing something it needs: clear ownership, a reliable process, the right expertise, or the authority to act.

The immediate problem might be a bad template, confused messaging, a recurring complaint, or a section of the site nobody can update without three teams, two agencies and a minor religious ceremony. The pattern matters more than the individual ticket.

Perhaps nobody owns performance, so every project negotiates it from scratch. Product marketing can list features but cannot articulate differentiation. Support knows why people are unhappy, but that knowledge never reaches product.

Organisations are good at disguising these weaknesses as queues of work. Twenty bad product descriptions become twenty copy tickets. Ten slow templates become ten performance tickets. Dashboards turn green; the underlying problem remains gainfully employed.

An audit should show which failures share a cause, who is absorbing the consequences, and what the organisation cannot currently do without specialist intervention. Otherwise it is just a more expensive backlog. Naming the gap does not close it; until somebody builds the missing capability, somebody else keeps absorbing the failure.

## [The cost of becoming indispensable](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-the-cost-of-becoming-indispensable)

Usually, those capability gaps are absorbed by a small group carrying the organisation’s institutional knowledge. Some dependence on those people is inevitable. The warning sign is when routine work depends on them steering projects around the same defects.

SEO knows which template breaks canonical tags, which dashboard is lying, which release process bypasses the checks, and who in engineering might get something fixed before 2050. Useful knowledge, certainly. Also a fairly damning description of the system.

Over time, the team becomes a manual exception layer, supported by spreadsheets, scripts and undocumented rituals. The cost is scattered across audits, meetings, escalations and repeated explanations. Each intervention looks tolerable, so nobody examines the total.

This is how a large organisation can employ an enormous SEO team while continuing to struggle with problems it should have solved years ago. More people give it more capacity to absorb the dysfunction; exactly the kind of accumulated advantage that lets [zombie companies](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/zombie-companies/) look healthy long after their capabilities have begun to decay.

The career incentives are unhelpful. Rescue a disastrous migration, and everybody knows about it. Make future migrations uneventful and, ideally, nobody notices. More involvement can look like influence when it really shows that the business cannot operate without supervision. The answer is not to supervise harder. It is to remove the failure from the process.

## [Designing the failure out](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-designing-the-failure-out)

The first time a migration destroys the internal linking, fixing the links is reasonable. By the third time, continuing to fix them is an admission that nobody intends to fix the migration process.

Most organisations measure activity: tickets closed, pages shipped, incidents resolved, projects completed. The broken thing gets repaired, and everybody moves on. Jira is very good at making recurrence look like progress.

The better response usually sits upstream. Metadata errors belong in templates. Performance requirements belong in the release process. Contradictory product information needs an owned source. A migration which depends on somebody remembering forty-seven fragile checks needs a different migration process.

This is not an argument for more governance. Large organisations already produce heroic quantities of process, much of it designed to demonstrate that the correct boxes were ticked shortly before something went wrong. The correction needs to live somewhere harder to ignore: a default, a test, a source of truth, an owner with the authority to act.

SEO can help identify the failure mode and specify what good looks like. That does not make us experts in platform engineering, product operations or organisational design. The people doing the work need to design and own the capability, or it will remain an SEO workaround with grander stationery.

This is also why handoff matters. SEO may introduce performance budgets or build the first monitoring system, but permanent ownership belongs with the team controlling the platform or product. Otherwise the bottleneck has merely moved.

Handing work back is uncomfortable. The receiving team may have worse judgement, less urgency or a distressing appetite for relearning expensive lessons. Things will regress. That is still healthier than making every meaningful decision wait for SEO approval.

A useful handoff leaves behind enough understanding, tooling and accountability for the capability to survive without constant permission. If it collapses when the SEO lead takes six months off, it was dependency in a nicer outfit. The proof of a successful handoff is not that the meeting happened; it is that the same class of failure stops coming back.

## [Measure what stops recurring](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-measure-what-stops-recurring)

Most SEO reporting rewards activity: audits completed, tickets closed, recommendations implemented, pages improved. Those numbers are easy to count. They can also describe an organisation standing perfectly still.

If the same class of issue keeps reappearing, closing more of it is throughput. The more useful measure is what stops coming back.

As capabilities improve, categories of intervention should disappear. Performance audits become less frequent because tests are built into delivery. Metadata reviews vanish because templates behave properly. Teams stop asking the same questions because the answers no longer live in somebody’s head.

This creates an awkward incentive. A team measured on tickets needs tickets. A consultancy paid for audits needs things to audit. An SEO function which proves its value through visible intervention has every reason to remain visibly involved.

Structural improvement produces fewer escalations, manual checks and meetings where somebody explains, again, why changing every URL might have consequences. It is harder to fit into the monthly deck, but visible in the organisation: work moves without waiting for SEO, and standards survive staff changes.

We should measure both. SEO still has commercial outcomes to influence, and not every intervention can or should disappear. But recurring remedial work is a poor sign of maturity, however efficiently the tickets are closed. A mature organisation needs less remedial SEO, not a more efficient dependency on it.

## [Make the fix unnecessary](https://www.jonoalderson.com/conjecture/organisational-dysfunction/#h-make-the-fix-unnecessary)

SEO does not need a grander title. It needs a better definition of success.

Its useful role is to connect signals that other teams see separately, expose recurring causes, and help put the correction in the part of the business able to own it. Then it should step back.

We should still fix the broken thing. But the point is to stop being needed for the same class of failure twice.

kept.heading: SHOULD YOU BUILD YOUR OWN AUDIENCE STACK IN THE AI ERA? (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI has made it much easier to build audience-platform features, but it hasn't eliminated the complexity of running them reliably. Building in-house still means maintaining integrations, sender reputation, and compliance over time. The decision should depend on whether a company has the resources to support the system long term, not just whether it can build the software cheaply. For many publishers, buying the infrastructure may still make more sense.

Title: Should you build your own audience stack in the AI era?

URL Source: https://digitalcontentnext.org/blog/2026/08/24/should-you-build-your-own-audience-stack-in-the-ai-era/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T11:23:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: -person at clean software dashboard with plumbing exposed underneath to show the difficult buy vs. build decision for an audience data platform-](https://digitalcontentnext.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/DashboardvsBuilding.jpg)

Publishers collect large amounts of valuable audience data and audience platforms have long helped publishers turn those signals into action. Lately, there’s a lot of talk about how AI can enhance these capabilities, but AI isn’t just changing what these platforms can do.

There’s a question moving through audience and product meetings right now, usually raised by someone sharp who just watched a developer ship in an afternoon what used to take a quarter: with AI tools this good, couldn’t we just build our own audience platform?

It’s a fair question, and it deserves a real answer rather than a defensive one. What follows is a way to work it out honestly: which layers of an audience stack AI genuinely compresses, which it does not, and five questions that move the decision off a software comparison and onto the operating reality where it lives. By the end you will know whether your organization is one of the few that should build — or one of the many that would ultimately regret it.

## **What genuinely changed**

Give AI its due first, because pretending it changes nothing would be inaccurate. AI has meaningfully compressed the cost of real work: moving data between systems, standing up a schema, building a query interface, generating a reporting screen. A small team with the right tools can now do those things faster than most people expected a year ago.

Here’s the catch. AI makes it much easier to build what an audience platform does. It doesn’t necessarily make it easier to operate everything that makes those capabilities work reliably. That asymmetry is central to the decision to build or buy.

## **The comparison that breaks the math**

The case for building your own often starts with an obvious savings: eliminate the vendor fee. But that cost doesn’t simply disappear. It shifts to the people required to build and maintain the system, manage every integration, and keep pace as your needs and the technology change.

And the thing you’d be building isn’t one product. When people picture “our own version,” they usually picture the one screen they live in: a query builder, a report, an email send. Underneath sits identity resolution across email, web, print, events, and forms; sending infrastructure with its own IP and domain reputation; journey orchestration; billing and payments; print fulfillment; consent and preference management; audit-grade reporting; a dozen live integrations; and the data hygiene that keeps all of it honest. That’s roughly 15 distinct systems, several highly regulated and at least one involving physical mail. And integrating them isn’t a one-time job. Each connection has to keep working as systems, requirements and regulations change. AI can make the code faster to write; it doesn’t eliminate the work of keeping everything connected.

Which points at the more useful question. The bottleneck in audience work was never really the software. According to Omeda’s [_State of Audience in Media 2026_](https://www.omeda.com/resources/reports/state-of-audience-2026/), only 9% of publishers use audience data extremely effectively to inform action. That gap isn’t a missing query tool. It’s everything around the tool — the accumulated data, the operational discipline, the trust that a number is right.

## **Five things you still own if you build your own**

If you’re weighing a build seriously, stress-test these, because they don’t get shorter no matter how good the code generation gets.

**Accumulated data.**Behavioral history, engagement recency, consent, and deliverability reputation are the output of years of observation. You can migrate a database; you can’t migrate a decade of behavior nobody was recording.

**Sender reputation.**IP and domain reputation is earned through sending history at the mailbox providers. A brand-new domain starts at zero no matter how elegant the tooling around it gets.

**Certification.**BPA and AAM don’t certify a codebase. They certify process, controls, and auditable records. A publisher whose audit depends on a homegrown system has put its rate card at risk.

**Regulated operations.**Payment processing under PCI, privacy obligations under a growing patchwork of state laws, and physical fulfillment all carry weight that has nothing to do with how good the software is.

**The integration surface.**Every connected system is a standing maintenance obligation. AI can write the integration; it doesn’t take the call when a vendor changes its API at 2 a.m.

## **Publishers have made this call before**

This decision comes around every decade, and the industry tends to land in the same place. Publishers left their own data centers for the cloud. They run an ad server they didn’t build. They process payments through a provider rather than carrying PCI themselves. Anyone who built a homegrown CMS in 2005 remembers how that aged. The logic each time: capital-intensive, compliance-heavy infrastructure only earns out at a scale a single publisher can’t reach alone, so it makes more sense to rent the plumbing and spend scarce engineering on what actually differentiates the business.

## **Some organizations should build**

A few genuinely should build. The profile fits a dedicated platform-engineering organization, an existing product-management function, in-house privacy counsel, security and compliance staff, and the willingness to fund all of it for 10 years, not 10 months. If that’s you, build with confidence.

The profile that will regret it looks different: a lean team already behind on the site and the paywall, no product manager to spare, privacy handled by whoever has time. The build will consume the people you needed for the work that grows revenue.

## **Five questions to ask before you build**

*   Who is on call at 6 a.m. when the morning send fails, and how fast can they fix it?
*   Who owns privacy governance for this — by name?
*   What happens when the person who built it leaves?
*   How many engineers are on your site, paywall, and integrations today — and is that enough?
*   When the next state privacy law passes, who reads it and who implements it?

If those answers come easily, you may be in the group that should build. If they make you wince, you’ve found the real cost and it’s one that never reaches the spreadsheet.

## **The point isn’t “don’t build”**

This isn’t an effort to convince you not to build. For some companies, it will be the right choice. The point is to compare the right things. The AI era has genuinely changed what a small team can create. It hasn’t changed what it takes to run an audience platform your revenue, your auditors, and your advertisers can depend on. Those are two different questions and confusing them is the expensive mistake.

kept.heading: MBA METRICS FOR SEO: HOW TO SPEAK LEADERSHIP'S LANGUAGE (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Leadership doesn't distrust SEO - it distrusts metrics reported in a language it was never trained to read. Rankings and traffic clicks mean nothing to a team that judges channels by market share and ROI, so the fix is translating SEO into those same terms. Share of Voice stands in for market share, organic traffic value stands in for revenue growth, and branded search volume stands in for brand demand. Reported this way, SEO stops being a marketing activity that needs defending and starts reading like a business one.

Title: MBA Metrics for SEO: How to Speak Leadership’s Language

URL Source: https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/

Published Time: 2026-08-24T15:52:49+00:00

Markdown Content:
Business leaders and decision-makers can easily distrust metrics they don’t understand or can't act on.

As an SEO professional, metrics like rankings, traffic, and clicks are meaningful to you, but to a leadership team trained on market share and return on investment, they're noise.

That's not a bias against SEO. It's just what happens when you report in a language leadership wasn't trained to read.

When your KPIs are metrics you don't recognize or don't know how to report on, leadership starts to doubt the numbers you do give them. Below are the SEO equivalents that let you speak their language with confidence.

## 1. Market share → Share of Voice

Market share is the percentage of total category revenue or demand that goes to your business instead of competitors.

Most leadership teams prioritize it in performance reports because it's the metric they use to judge whether a marketing channel, campaign, or strategy is winning or losing.

If your market share is climbing while competitors' is shrinking, that signals growth and that what you're doing is working.

If your revenue or traffic is growing but your share stays flat or slips, the market could be growing faster than you are, and competitors are capturing more of that growth than you are.

SEO doesn't have a native way to track market share (which is exactly why "rankings" and "traffic" don't land the same way in a leadership meeting).

However, market share [correlates quite strongly](https://hbr.org/1990/01/ad-spending-maintaining-market-share) with [Share of Voice](https://ahrefs.com/blog/share-of-voice/), which measures the percentage of organic clicks you get across a set of keywords, relative to your competitors.

[Research by James Hankins](https://ipa.co.uk/news/share-of-search), spanning 30 case studies across 12 categories and seven countries, found that share of search accounts for roughly 83% of a brand's market share (a pattern surfaced in [earlier research](https://ipa.co.uk/news/binet-presents-fast-cheap-predictive-share-of-search-metric) from Les Binet).

In short, when your Share of Voice moves, your market share tends to follow.

Reporting on Share of Voice reframes the question from "are we ranking" to "how much of the market are we actually winning?"

This is a market share question, asked in market share terms.

You can track Share of Voice directly in Ahrefs' [Rank Tracker](https://ahrefs.com/rank-tracker), so there's no manual calculation involved, and it's a number you can drop straight into a leadership report as-is.

AI Share of Voice, tracked in Ahrefs' [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar), applies the same logic to AI search — how often your brand shows up in answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI Overviews, relative to competitors.

Ideally, you want to see Share of Voice sitting above your market share. The wider that lead, the more market share tends to follow, and that’s how you’ll grow your share over time to get ahead of the competition.

You can do this by:

*   [**Ranking for a wider share of your keyword set**](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-to-use-keywords-for-seo/)**:** Share of Voice is measured across your tracked keywords. The more of them you rank well for, the bigger your slice of available clicks.
*   [**Publishing more consistently than competitors**](https://ahrefs.com/blog/content-calendar/)**:** Visibility compounds with output. A steady cadence means more pages competing over time, while sporadic competitors leave gaps you can claim first.
*   [**Going after the terms competitors currently own**](https://ahrefs.com/blog/keyword-competitive-analysis)**:** Share of Voice is zero-sum. Every keyword a competitor outranks you on is a share you're not capturing. So, if you claim more visibility for their top terms, it improves your Share of Voice.

One caveat worth flagging is that growing Share of Voice is not a "just spend more" rule for everyone.

Smaller brands typically need to overspend just to hold their ground, while larger brands can sustain a lower share of voice than market share and still be fine.

## [](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/) 2. Revenue growth rate → organic traffic value

Revenue growth rate is the percentage change in revenue over a given period, and most organizations already track it at the company level.

The problem is attributing it to a specific channel, which is genuinely hard in SEO. Organic attribution was never clean, and AI-driven search is making it messier, since a chunk of that influence never shows up as a trackable click at all.

Therefore, if you’re not already tracking organic revenue growth, try measuring growth in Organic Traffic Value instead.

It’s the practical middle ground. It's not revenue, but it's a dollar figure that represents how much your organic traffic would cost if you used paid ads to generate it.

It’s calculated directly in Ahrefs [Site Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/site-explorer) from your keyword rankings and CPC data.

Track its trend over time using the Performance graph in Site Explorer, and you've got a decent stand-in for revenue growth rate that leadership can work with. Just search your site, no analytics setup required.

## [](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/) 3. Market penetration → Share of Traffic Value

Market penetration asks whether you are capturing more of the market over time, or just growing in absolute terms.

SEO reporting usually botches this distinction. Traffic goes up and to the right, and it looks like growth.

But that doesn't answer the question leadership's actually asking: are you winning share, or did the market just get bigger?

Those are two separate checks.

To check whether the market is growing, pull up your category or topic in Ahrefs' [Keywords Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/keywords-explorer) and track how search volume and traffic potential trend over time.

Don't just judge it off a single keyword though. One term's search volume is a sample point, not the market.

Build out a keyword cluster by grouping relevant matching terms, questions people are asking, and terms you (or competitors) already rank for alongside it.

Add these to your list, then look at the aggregate volume and traffic potential across the whole cluster over time, not any single row in isolation.

That aggregate trend is what tells you whether total demand for the category is trending up, flat, or down.

Ahrefs'[search demand lifecycle](https://ahrefs.com/blog/search-demand-lifecycle/) framework is worth a look here too. It breaks demand into phases (growing, peaking, plateauing, declining), so you're not just checking direction; you're checking where the category actually sits in its life cycle.

That phase changes how you should read your own numbers.

Growing share in a declining category, for example, is still a win worth calling out to leadership. You're capturing more of a shrinking pie, even if the topline traffic number is flat or falling.

But, if your traffic and revenue are growing as a natural consequence of the market growing, there's a hidden risk you may be unaware of. You might be capturing less of the new market opportunity than competitors, and in this case, you’re actually running behind.

This is where it helps to track metrics like Share of Traffic Value (SoTV).

*   **Share of Voice** (from Section 1) tells you what percentage of clicks you're capturing, relative to competitors.
*   **Share of Traffic Value (SoTV)** tells you what percentage of the dollar opportunity you're capturing — the same logic as Traffic Value above, but measured competitively instead of in isolation.

Ahrefs calculates SoTV in Site Explorer, with no analytics setup required. Just enter your competitors:

Then analyze each brand’s performance. The graph will look like this:

This is a stacked share chart where all sites always add to 100%, so one site's gain is another's loss, even if absolute traffic never changed.

Read it as relative position, not absolute performance: mayoclinic.org has grown share since 2020, while healthline.com, webmd.com and medicalnewstoday.com have shrunk. When presenting this to your stakeholders, be clear that it shows who's winning ground, not whether any site's actual traffic value is rising or falling.

This is exactly the kind of story a raw traffic chart can't tell you.

Deeper insights about your market position and penetration, relative to the opportunity in your industry, are more meaningful conversations to have with leadership than simply showing rankings or traffic increasing.

## [](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/) 4. Customer lifetime value → organic engagement signals

Leadership may track metrics like customer lifetime value (CLV) and retention because acquiring a customer is one thing, but keeping them, and knowing they were worth acquiring, is another.

SEO doesn't have a clean number for either.

What it can offer instead is a set of signals showing whether organic-sourced customers behave differently from customers from other channels. It’s often a better starting point than forcing a CLV figure out of imperfect attribution.

In this case, you’re comparing engagement, not acquisition. In GA4, segment sessions by channel and look at time on site, pages per session, and bounce rate for organic versus paid, social, and direct.

You can also use Ahrefs’ Web Analytics for a privacy-friendly alternative to GA4.

If organic visitors consistently stick around longer or browse more pages, that indicates they're a better-qualified audience.

In Web Analytics, you can also track visitors from AI platforms as a separate segment and report on this separately to curious stakeholders.

For ecommerce, you can go a step further by comparing average order value and repeat purchase rate by acquisition channel. You’ll need to set up your analytics platform to track revenue and sales to capture these insights.

If organic customers spend more per order, or come back to buy again more often, that's a compelling retention story that speaks in the same terms as CLV, without needing a detailed attribution model to prove it.

In any of the above situations, you’ll need to be upfront about the limits.

None of this is causal proof, and it's not a substitute for a properly attributed CLV number if your organization can build one. But when clean attribution isn't realistic, these comparisons give leadership something concrete to look at to better understand SEO’s impact, rather than nothing.

## [](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/) 5. Brand demand → branded search

Brand demand is the number of people actively seeking your brand by name, rather than discovering it through a category search. For example, it’s the difference between someone talking or thinking about “Asana” instead of "project management software."

Leadership tracks it as a core marketing metric because it's demand you didn't have to fight competitors for. It’s also a tangible way to measure marketing activities that build brand awareness.

It's rarely built in search, though. Instead, it’s built through social, word-of-mouth, ads, press, and product experience. People discover a brand elsewhere, then Google it.

The clearest way to track that is with branded search volume, which measures how many people search your brand name (and close variants) each month. Pull this directly from Ahrefs' Keywords Explorer by searching your brand name.

You can also build a list of branded variants for a more holistic picture:

It also works for local businesses. This plumbing business, for instance, earns 900+ branded searches every month.

Tracked over time, it's a decent proxy for whether your other marketing efforts are actively improving brand demand or not.

A PR push, a rebrand, a big social moment — if it's landing, more people search your brand name afterward. That's validation you can hand back to marketing leaders, even when SEO didn't drive the campaign.

That first post-discovery search is where the decision actually gets made.

Someone's heard your name, seen your ad, or gotten a recommendation, and now they're checking you out before they commit. If they like what they see on their first search for your brand, [you capture demand](https://ahrefs.com/blog/demand-capture-seo/). If they don’t, you lose it, often to a competitor riding on your brand's coattails.

A few ways branded search goes badly:

*   You don't rank for your own brand name
*   Competitors, affiliates, or stockists outrank you on your own branded terms
*   AI answers surface outdated or incorrect information about your brand
*   Negative press or reviews dominate the results page

Every one of these is fixable with SEO and reputation management.

## [](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mba-metrics-for-seo/)Final thoughts

Every metric in this piece is a correlation or a leading indicator, not a guarantee. Say that out loud every time you present them. The fastest way to lose credibility with a leadership team is to overstate what a metric proves.

Used honestly, though, these translations between MBA metrics and SEO metrics let you stop defending SEO as a marketing activity and start reporting it as a business one.

Pick one metric from this list and map it against your own data this week. It's a small exercise, and it'll change how your next leadership update lands.

kept.heading: META SETTLES SOCIAL MEDIA ADDICTION CASE WITH CALIFORNIA, OTHER STATES FOR $16.7 BILLION (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Meta's settlement doesn't just bind Meta. States are set to keep 70% of the $16.7 billion payout regardless, but the remaining 30% only unlocks if Google's YouTube and TikTok adopt the same kind of daily time limits, age-assurance checks, and night mode Meta is now required to build. Title: Meta settles social media addiction case with California, other states for $16.7 billion

URL Source: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/26/meta-social-media-trial-settlement.html

Published Time: 2026-08-26T13:05:31+0000

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Meta settles social media addiction trial with California, other states](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108354472-17877496121787749609-47996359201-1080pnbcnews.jpg?v=1787749611&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

watch now

[Meta](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/META/) and a coalition of state attorneys general have settled a major federal case centering on allegations that the [social media](https://www.cnbc.com/social-media/) giant misrepresented the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like [Facebook and Instagram](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/25/instagram-adam-mosseri-testifies-california-state-ag-federal-meta.html).

The settlement was revealed in a court filing released Wednesday that details several requirements Meta must make to its apps as part of a proposed “consent judgement.” The court officially approved the settlement later in the afternoon, according to a legal filing signed by Northern District of California Judge [Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/22/meet-yvonne-gonzalez-rogers-judge-taking-on-meta.html).

Those changes include daily usage limits and “nighttime blocks” for teenagers who use the company’s apps, “enhanced age assurance measures” that would prevent children from using them, and the creation of additional tools for parents and guardians.

As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to pay $16.7 billion. The state of California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion as part of the settlement, according to an announcement by California Attorney General [Rob Bonta](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/18/meta-attorneys-general-opening-arguments-california-bonta-restitution.html). Texas was not part of the group settlement and agreed to a $1 billion payment separately.

“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Bonta said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months.”

Several state AG’s touted a $17.1 billion settlement amount. That number includes more than $459 million for claims related to the Cambridge Analytica matter which dates back to 2018 and was separate from the child safety case.

Each party waived “all rights to appeal this Final Judgment,” the filing states.

## Read more CNBC tech news

*   [Meta settles social media addiction case with California, other states for $16.7 billion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/26/meta-social-media-trial-settlement.html)
*   [HP partners with U.S.-blacklisted Huawei for licensing the Chinese company’s WiFi tech](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/25/hp-partners-huawei-wifi-tech-us-entity-list.html)
*   [Amazon service Bezos once called ‘artificial artificial intelligence’ is shutting down](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/25/amazon-service-that-jeff-bezos-called-artificial-ai-is-shutting-down.html)
*   [OpenAI data center chief Chris Malone is out, the latest in a string of executive exits](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/25/openais-head-of-data-centers-chris-malone-is-out-in-latest-exec-exit.html)

Meta shares rose about 1% as of early afternoon. [Snap](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/SNAP/), which is subject to the broader effort by AGs to force changes at social media companies, saw its stock sink more than 8%.

The trial, which kicked off with opening arguments last week, was being held at the Oakland federal courthouse in California. It was co-led by Bonta and the AGs from Colorado, New Jersey and Kentucky, who represented a [bipartisan group](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/10/24/metas-harmful-effects-on-children-unites-republicans-and-democrats.html) of 29 AGs in a combined case stemming from a 2023 lawsuit.

The trial has been suspended pending review of the agreement between the parties, according to a court spokesperson.

In Bonta’s announcement detailing the settlement, he noted that the effort involved a “bipartisan coalition of 51 attorneys general.”

Meta said the settlement agreement “includes a payment of approximately $18 billion,” which will be “distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period.” That money will fund various youth online safety initiatives as deemed by the states.

The “participating states” will receive about $12.7 billion, or 70%, of the total settlement payment over the next 10 years, Meta said. Those states can receive the remaining $5.3 billion, or 30%, as long as [Google](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/GOOGL/)’s YouTube and TikTok implement certain app changes, such as daily time limits for youth, age-assurance measures, and a “night mode.” Meta’s rivals must also agree to all pay an amount that matches the remaining 30%, “with half of the remaining funds tied to YouTube’s payment and half tied to TikTok’s.”

![Image 2: Meta settlement 'imposes significant regulatory changes,' says fmr. Assistant AG Jonathan Kanter](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108354507-17877532331787753230-47997214383-1080pnbcnews.jpg?v=1787753232&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

watch now

Meta said it expects to “accrue a legal expense of approximately $10 billion in the third quarter of 2026 related to the agreement,” which was not previously taken into account.

The only notable executive to appear for Meta was Instagram chief Adam Mosseri, who testified on Tuesday that he [doesn’t direct employees](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/25/instagram-adam-mosseri-testifies-california-state-ag-federal-meta.html) to withhold certain child-safety and product information from him to provide cover and mislead the public. Meta CEO [Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.cnbc.com/mark-zuckerberg/) was slated to potentially testify later in the trial.

The settlement is the biggest yet for Meta, but not the only one it’s been force to pay.

Earlier in August, A New Mexico judge ordered [Meta to contribute $567 million](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/06/meta-to-pay-into-567-million-fund-after-child-harms-case-new-mexico.html) to an abatement fund as part of a [public nuisance case](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/04/meta-new-mexico-child-safety-facebook-instagram.html) centering on child-safety allegations. The judge’s ruling came several months after a New Mexico jury [decided](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/24/jury-reaches-verdict-in-meta-child-safety-trial-in-new-mexico.html) that Meta should pay $375 million in damages based on the number of times it violated the state’s unfair practices act.

Other cases against Meta are still playing out, including one involving social media personal injury claims and a consolidated, nationwide federal school district case.

“Thousands of young people and public school districts still have claims pending in the MDL against Meta, as well as TikTok, Snap and YouTube, and we stand ready to continue that fight,” lawyers representing the plaintiffs in those cases said in a statement Wednesday. “We will not rest until every one of these plaintiffs sees justice for the harms caused by all of the defendants’ platforms.”
