# When AI answer engines quote a person, that person is on LinkedIn 74% of the time

[Marketing Intelligence](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/marketing-intelligence/)Published: August 26, 2026

[![Image 16: Daniel Kushner](https://www.oktopost.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Daniel-Kushner.png) Daniel Kushner](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/author/daniel/)

Share[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.oktopost.com%2Fblog%2Flinkedin-ai-citations%2F)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.oktopost.com%2Fblog%2Flinkedin-ai-citations%2F&text=When+AI+answer+engines+quote+a+person%2C+that+person+is+on+LinkedIn+74%25+of+the+time)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.oktopost.com%2Fblog%2Flinkedin-ai-citations%2F&title=When+AI+answer+engines+quote+a+person%2C+that+person+is+on+LinkedIn+74%25+of+the+time)

![Image 17: When AI answer engines quote a person, that person is on LinkedIn 74% of the time](https://www.oktopost.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/31883-When-AI-answer-engines-quote-a-person-that-person-is-on-LinkedIn-74-of-the-time-715x357.png)

### Table of contents

*   [What this means for your social program](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/linkedin-ai-citations/#what-this-means-for-your-social-program)
*   [The Reddit question](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/linkedin-ai-citations/#the-reddit-question)
*   [The numbers behind this](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/linkedin-ai-citations/#the-numbers-behind-this)
*   [What to do with this](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/linkedin-ai-citations/#what-to-do-with-this)
*   [An advocacy program is the mechanism](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/linkedin-ai-citations/#an-advocacy-program-is-the-mechanism)

We ran an audit of 63 B2B companies to see where AI answer engines pull their social sources from. One number stood out. When those engines quote a named person, not a company, not a forum thread, a person, that person published on LinkedIn 74% of the time.

It’s our own audit, not a published research study, so treat the numbers as a snapshot of what we found.

B2B buyers are already asking AI answer engines to summarize a category before they talk to a salesperson. Marketing teams have started tracking how often their brand shows up in those answers, the same instinct that drove a decade of SEO work. Most of that tracking focuses on which sources get cited most often overall. Our audit asked a narrower question: when the answer includes a named person’s opinion, where did that person publish it?

AI answer engines don’t just cite sources. They cite people. A model answering “what do B2B marketers think about X” wants a name attached to the opinion. Across the 63 companies in our audit, we counted every named voice the engines quoted outside of Reddit’s community threads. There were 385 of them. LinkedIn accounted for 285 of those citations. Medium was next, at 12.5%. Substack came in at 4.9%. Quora and Hacker News tied at 3.1% each. SlideShare took 1.6%, and X took 0.5%.

LinkedIn wasn’t close on this measure. It was cited for 52 of the 63 companies we audited, 83% of them, more companies than any other network.

## What this means for your social program

If your company has a point of view worth quoting, LinkedIn is where AI answer engines expect to find the person holding it. A company blog post can inform a model. A LinkedIn post from your VP of product, your head of sales, or your founder gives the model a name to cite.

This changes how you should think about your social program. A company page builds the audience and sets the record straight on what your brand stands for. But company pages made up only 6.7% of the social citations in our audit. Individual posts by named people made up 32.8%. We dug into that split separately in [who AI actually cites, your employees or your company page](https://www.oktopost.com/blog/ai-answer-engines-cite-employees-more-than-company-page/). Your experts, publishing under their own names, are doing work your company page can’t do on its own.

Think about why a model would prefer a named source in the first place. An answer engine assembling a response wants to attribute a claim to someone accountable for it. A company page speaks for the brand in aggregate. A named post carries a person’s credibility, their job title, their history of posts on the topic. That’s easier for a model to cite as “according to [name], [title] at [company]” than to attribute a general company statement the same way.

## The Reddit question

Reddit is the single largest source of social citations in our audit, at 55.8% of all social citations. Almost all of that is community discussion, threads and comments from many contributors rather than a named individual making a claim. That’s a different kind of source than a person publishing an opinion piece. Community discussion answers “what are people saying.” A named LinkedIn post answers “what does this specific person think, and can I attribute it to them.”

Both matter to an AI answer engine building an answer. But if your goal is getting your own experts quoted by name, Reddit’s community threads aren’t where that happens for most B2B companies. LinkedIn is.

## The numbers behind this

Some context on scale. Across the 63 B2B companies in our audit, we tracked 27,181 total citations from AI answer engines. Social sources accounted for 2,720 of them, 10.0% of everything cited. Of those social citations, community discussion (mostly Reddit) made up 58.9%, individual posts made up 32.8%, and company pages made up 6.7%.

Social is a minority of citations overall. Most of what an AI answer engine cites still comes from owned content, review sites, and press coverage. But social is the layer where a named person can show up in the answer at all. A blog post gets attributed to the company. A LinkedIn post can get attributed to the person who wrote it, by name and title.

Put those together and the pattern is specific: when an AI answer engine wants a community’s general sentiment, it pulls from Reddit threads. When it wants a named expert’s opinion, it pulls from LinkedIn 74% of the time. Those are two different jobs, and LinkedIn is winning the one that puts your people’s names in the answer.

## What to do with this

The practical takeaway isn’t “post more on LinkedIn.” It’s “get more of your named experts publishing on LinkedIn under their own names, on the topics you want AI answer engines to associate with your company.”

A few starting points:

*   **Identify your quotable experts.** Who at your company has a real opinion on the topics your buyers ask AI answer engines about? Product leaders, sales leaders, and subject-matter experts are the most citable, not just the CEO.
*   **Publish under their names, not just the company page.** Company pages have their place. They’re not where citations concentrate.
*   **Cover the specific questions your buyers ask.** A named post that directly answers a real buyer question is more citable than a general thought-leadership piece.
*   **Check where you stand today.** Oktopost’s [free AI visibility audit](https://www.oktopost.com/tools/ai-visibility-audit/) shows which AI answer engines already cite your company. It also shows which competitor voices are showing up instead of yours.

## An advocacy program is the mechanism

Getting one executive to post occasionally won’t move a citation count. Getting a dozen named experts publishing consistently will.

A structured employee advocacy program is how that happens at scale. It gives your product leaders, sales leaders, and subject-matter experts a steady supply of content to post under their own names, without asking each of them to become a full-time writer. It also gives marketing visibility into what’s actually going out, which matters for compliance and consistency once more than one or two people are posting regularly.

None of this replaces a strong company page or a good content strategy. It sits alongside them. The company page still carries your brand voice and reaches people who follow the company directly. What the advocacy layer adds is the named, attributable voice that AI answer engines are already pulling into their answers three times out of four when a person, not a page, gets quoted.

Run the [free AI visibility audit](https://www.oktopost.com/tools/ai-visibility-audit/) to see where your company stands. It shows which named voices AI answer engines are already surfacing in your category, and where the gaps are against competitors doing this well.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do AI answer engines cite LinkedIn more than other networks overall?

Our audit measured something more specific than overall network volume: when an AI answer engine quotes a named person rather than a community thread, that person published on LinkedIn 74% of the time. That is a citation-by-person measure, not a ranking of every network's overall volume.

### What role does Reddit play in AI answer engine citations?

Reddit is the largest single source of social citations in our audit, at 55.8%. Almost all of it is community discussion rather than a named individual's post, so it answers a different question for the model: general sentiment rather than an attributable expert opinion.

### Should we stop posting from our company LinkedIn page?

No. Company pages set the record on what your brand stands for and build the audience your experts post into. They made up 6.7% of the social citations we tracked, while individual posts made up 32.8%. Both play a role.

### How many companies did this audit cover?

63 B2B companies, 27,181 total citations across all source types, with 2,720 of those from social sources.

Published Time: 2026-08-24T12:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Hey friends,

First, a quick personal update.

Things have been going insanely well at Ad Juice.

I hit capacity within the first month and still have consistent inbound coming in.

As a result, I’ve been head down working on client accounts and didn’t spend as much time on personal content.

To make it up to you all, I’m making this one super action packed.

We’re covering the 5 most effective strategies for generating pipeline in Q3 so far.

It’s an honest roundup of what’s working and what isn’t for the accounts I’m working on right now.

Some of them are pretty surprising and go against a lot of conventional LinkedIn Ads wisdom.

Let’s get stuck into it with tactic #1.

## Tactic #1 — 3rd Party Targeting + LAN

This one is gonna blow your minds (it blew mine).

Everybody says don’t touch LAN (LinkedIn Audience Network). I used to say the same thing but I never actually tested it.

I’m not a fan of blindly accepting conventional wisdom because so many people just regurgitate what they’ve heard other people say like it’s gospel. I prefer to test for myself and make my own mind up.

It makes sense to avoid LAN if you’re using LinkedIn’s native audience filters. They’re already serving your ads using crap inventory, why add more with LAN?

BUT, if you’re using 3rd party audiences YOU KNOW are high quality, wouldn’t LAN just get you more overall reach and visibility, across more devices, and lead to better results?

That was the logic, so I tested it.

And the results look dope.

7 inbound over 90 days and 2 qualified leads that converted to pipeline (the result probably will too, it’s a 60-day ish sales cycle).

The non-LAN campaign? 1 inbound over the same period from the same spend 🤯

The 2 campaigns were setup pretty much the same. Same audience. Same bid strategy. Only difference was one had LAN, one didn’t.

The LAN variation had slightly higher reach and frequency due to a lower uCPM (cost per 1,000 impressions/unique CPM).

It was also a “cold” campaign, not retargeting.

Now, I wouldn’t recommend just anybody try this.

If you’re not using laser-focused 3rd party audiences from a tool like Clay or Primer, it will waste your budget on irrelevant impressions.

## Tactic #2 — Ungated Case Study Doc Ads

I’ve always been a big fan of ungated doc ads.

But, this quarter, I’ve been experimenting with running them as case studies.

The way it works is fairly straightforward, you create a standard LinkedIn PDF document in 4:5.

Then, on the front cover, you lead with a hook that communicates a desirable outcome prospective customers might want based on a real result an existing customer achieved.

The next few slides then outline the steps or actions that helped the customer achieve the result.

The final slide is always a soft CTA letting any in-market prospects know what to do next if they want to work with you.

I like to add a link to the book a meeting/demo page in the primary copy too for anybody who’s feeling impulsive.

For ad set setup, I tend to favour the engagement objective. But, awareness would probably work here too.

In terms of results, one client saw 3 inbound within the first month, and one converted directly to a qualified opp.

For another, it ended up being their highest engagement rate document within week 1 with 20%+ vs ~10% for all the other “how to” style docs we were running. So I’m fairly confident that’ll convert to pipeline over the next few weeks too.

I’m in the process of rolling out this tactic for all my clients now as it’s looking so promising.

## Tactic #3 — Classic low-intent lead generation

I decided to start testing this after a different experiment failed.

Everybody says you should ungate everything, right? Well, we tried it with an extremely valuable asset for one of my clients.

The big problem was literally 1 person interacted with it. For whatever reason, prospects just didn’t see the value when it was ungated.

So, we put that same asset behind a gate and ran 2 website visits campaigns to the landing page:

*   Thought leader ads campaign

*   Message ads campaign

We’ve had 15 sign ups in the last 30 days alone, with a $90 CPL for TLAs and a $50 CPL for the message ads. Both results are extremely efficient.

Even though it’s low-intent, we’ve already seen those same campaigns generating qualified inbound too.

We just launched this last week for another client and it’s generated 2 qualified inbound from target accounts (not yet pipeline, but a good start).

Now, similar to the LAN experiment, this will fail if your targeting isn’t dialled in.

I actually suspect the reason those spammy MQLs never converted for so many B2Bs is more to do with bad targeting than because the strategy itself was broken.

Here’s a few of the low-intent offers that have worked:

*   Short email nurture sequences around a specific pain point

*   Webinars

*   Calculators

*   Free gift cards + low-intent interview research request

*   Twist on a demo

I also tried to incentivise an account list to join our webinar as a panel guest with this strategy, but it totally bombed.

The trick is definitely in making all the upside on your audience’s end.

## Tactic 4 — TLA preview links

Every now and then, you stumble on a winning tactic by accident. This is one of those times.

We were running promo for one of the lead gen campaigns above and forgot to remove the preview link from the thought leaders post.

I decided to run it anyway and see what happened.

Turns out it was a good idea.

From the same spend, that variation of the ad had 4X more inbound than any of the others in the campaign.

It wasn’t a one off either.

On a separate campaign to a different segment, the same thing happened — 2X more inbound vs any of the other ads from the same spend across all the ads.

For setup, both campaigns were running engagement objective, set to manual bidding.

I’m also running this under additional testing for all my other clients to see how it holds up across audiences and industries.

## Tactic 5 — Single Image TLAs

One of the biggest battles I’ve had with thought leader ads is that yes, you get more engagement, but, without branded assets, I wondered if you’re actually building long-term mental availability and only capturing in-market demand.

So, lately, I’ve been experimenting with TLAs that use typical branded single images so we get the best of both worlds:

1.   High engagement and low CPM of TLAs

2.   Mental availability of product marketing ads to build mental availability

Does it work for the intended purpose? It’s hard to say.

I’m not at the stage with any accounts where we’re meaningfully measuring mental availability (although I am working on a cheap way to do this).

That said, the initial results look good.

Out of a set of 10 ads, this format is the only one to generate inbound leads. The other TLAs with regular images didn’t and neither did the regular branded single image ads.

I’m not a huge fan of using engagement rate to measure ad effectiveness. BUT, it’s still a useful signal. We also saw a 2X higher engagement rate vs the campaign average with this format.

Looks promising, so it’s at least worth a 6-8 week test vs your other formats to see how it performs.

## That’s a wrap

Okay folks, that’s everything from me. Hopefully there’s enough useful info there to make up for a few weeks of radio silence.

I’m gonna aim to keep up a more consistent schedule, but, honestly, I sometimes like to have a little more time in between editions as it gives me time to actually test some new stuff instead of paraphrasing the same info.

I’ll aim for a bi-weekly cadence going forward, which should be a good balance and easier to manage with the client load.

Thanks for reading and catch ya in the next one 🤘

P.P.S. I’m thinking of launching a small community for LinkedIn Ads operators. It would be low-cost (<$100/mo), then I’ll do a bi-weekly office hours where you can bring your LinkedIn problems, ideas, and thoughts, and I’ll offer feedback on them in real-time. Then, there would be a Slack channel where you can hit me with any Qs in between sessions as they come up. Respond “interested” to this email if it’s something you’d be interested in and I’ll explore setting it up.

A field kit for new demand gen leaders. I’ll walk you through the plan I built when I joined Vector, the parts that didn’t survive contact with the job, and (most importantly) the playbook I’d hand someone starting fresh.

I’ll save you a lot of stress by saying that up front. I wrote a thorough 30-60-90 before I joined Vector. Spoiler alert: it didn’t survive its original form. Some of it didn’t survive the first month, some of it got pushed, and some of it got dropped entirely. And then there were things I didn’t plan for that ended up mattering more than I expected.

Demand gen at an early-stage company moves fast on every front: the market, the product, the team, the buyer. The plan is a useful starting point. The work is figuring out what to keep and what to throw out as you go.

What I want to give you here is the version of my 90 days I’d write knowing what I know now—the one with the trade-offs and the things I’d actually do differently.

Moving manual attribution to a reporting tool

A few things to know about the context:

*   I joined Vector as the first demand gen hire in seat. If you’re walking into something similar, the playbook below maps closely. If you’re at a Series C with an existing team, the timelines compress, but the experimentation mindset still applies. Early-stage forces you to ship fast and learn from live campaigns instead of planning in circles, and that’s worth borrowing regardless of stage.
*   Most of this is anchored in the early-stage startup reality: small team, real pipeline pressure, a stack you’ll need to build and not just inherit.
*   I’ll be honest about what worked and what didn’t. That’s the only version of this that’s useful.

I’ll probably get some hate for this, but I’ll say it anyway: most new demand gen hires over-index on perfect attribution and perfect dashboards before anything is actually live. The instinct is to defend the work that hasn’t happened yet, but the cost is the first 60 days of momentum.

You need enough attribution to know what’s working directionally. You don’t need a fully built attribution platform with multi-touch and customer journey mapping before your first brand campaign goes live. Those are great things to have, but they’re not blockers.

The reframe I’d offer: get the directional reporting infrastructure in place, ship campaigns fast, then build the more sophisticated layers in parallel. If pipeline is growing, you don’t need to defend a dashboard.

Strategy doc and live campaigns by week three

Dashboards built to inform, in phases

*   ![Image 27](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/666c800c0d49f944831ac2e5/6a54a91339c26a374593b570_Group%20130.svg)

Focus on the work, the rest will follow

Hot Take

If your pipeline is producing, no one cares about your dashboard. At least not at the stage most new demand gen hires walk into.

![Image 28](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/666c800c0d49f944831ac2e5/6a5584f3d66a75f86ff5e58c_hot-take-icon.png)

Six things worth doing before you do anything else. If I could hand a new demand gen hire a single piece of paper on their first Monday, this would be it.

*   Meet as many people on the team as you can. 
Sales, CS, product, ops. Especially marketing ops, if that's a separate function. You'll need them more than you think. 
*   Watch sales calls. A lot of them. 
I watched 20 to 30 in my first month. You're listening for the language buyers use to describe the problem, not the language sales uses to pitch it. 
*   Watch CS kickoff calls too. 
This is where buyers restate, in their own words, why they bought. Best free positioning research you'll ever do. 
*   Audit how the market sees you. 
Pull Google Search Console and see what you index for, what competitors say about you, what customers say on LinkedIn. Where are you findable? Where are you not? 
*   Audit your CRM and ad accounts. 
Especially if you weren't the one who set them up. You don't have to fix it all in week one, but you should know what's broken. 
*   Run a creative inventory. 
What videos, copy, decks, landing pages already exist that you could repurpose into a campaign this month? The answer is usually more than you think. 

Three priorities for the first month. In this order, and not necessarily one at a time.

1

### Get into the product

Use it. Demo it back to yourself. Find a way to be an actual customer of your own product in week one. I shipped two campaigns in my first week in role because I wanted to feel what our buyers feel when they use Vector. The sales calls I sat in after that made a lot more sense.

2

### Listen for language, not just pain.

The pain points matter, but the words buyers use to describe them matter more. At Vector I found a gap pretty quickly between how sales was pitching the product and how customers were actually talking about the problem they’d hired us to solve. That gap is worth looking for at any company you join. It usually tells you something the messaging hasn’t caught up to yet.

One useful early test for that gap is a competitor conquest campaign, running ads against the established names in your category to see how your product positions next to them. You capture some of their traffic, and you learn how your product positions when it's sitting next to theirs.

You’ll find that gap somewhere too. It might be in how customers describe the problem, the role they’re hiring for, or the workflow they’re trying to fix. Write it down.

3

### Run a creative audit, then ship.

Before you build anything new, find out what’s already there. At Vector, that meant looking at content the team had built before I got there. It also meant having a candid conversation about what our budget could do for us. The campaigns I shipped in month one used a mix of both. I had two live by the end of week one, because the creative was there and waiting.

What shipped in week one

2

Campaigns went live

Using creative that already existed. The goal wasn't to prove the strategy, but to start learning from something live.

What came later

The multi-channel play

CTV, YouTube, LinkedIn feed ads, all running against the same ICP audience. That came after I understood what was working and why. You can’t build the [surround sound](https://www.vector.co/blog/vector-on-vector-surround-sound-marketing) play in week one, but you can build the foundation.

4

### Pick one channel, maybe two

Pick wherever your ICP actually lives. For most B2B teams, that’s Google or LinkedIn or both. I heavily invested in LinkedIn—quite a bit more than Google, about a 70/30 split—because we had momentum on LinkedIn organic, and I knew our ICP was very active on that channel. If I didn’t have that reason, I would have just started with one and focused on getting the most out of the channel.

The temptation when you’re new is to hedge and launch everywhere at once, but it doesn’t work. You learn less from five channels at half-effort than from one channel you actually understand. You can always add. You can’t get back the budget you spent proving that.

This is the tricky part of the 90 days. Campaigns are live and you're watching numbers daily, but nothing has compounded yet. Meanwhile, leadership is asking what's working.

Paid platforms need somewhere between two and four weeks to optimize before you can fairly judge a strategy. You can usually read creative performance within a week. You can usually read audience and targeting issues within two. But anything that requires the platform to actually learn (and most do) needs longer.

I'd tell every new demand gen hire to **say this out loud to leadership before they ask:**"I'm spending the first 30 days understanding the company, the market, and building the strategy. The second 30, I need to give the platforms time to learn. We'll judge what's working at the 60 to 90 day mark." If you set that expectation up front, you'll get the runway you need. If you don't, you'll spend month two playing defense.

Week 1 of a new campaign

**Read the creative**

If the ad isn’t pulling clicks at all, the creative is wrong. The fix is fast and the signal is loud. If you're getting clicks but no conversions, then you need to take a look at your landing page messaging and conversion rate optimization.

Week 2 of a new campaign

Read the audience

If you’re getting clicks but no relevant buyers are coming to the website, your targeting or audience definition is off. Use website de-anonymization to triage. Tighten before you scale.

Week 3-4 of a new campaign

Read the strategy

By now the platform has had time to optimize. What you’re seeing in the numbers is the real signal of whether this campaign works.

### What you can build by the end of month two.

If the creative audit went well and you have enough data to tell you that you’re directionally producing results, the natural next layer is connecting your campaigns into shared audience structures that feed into each other. This is where compound interest can build. Multiple creative formats and multiple different campaigns and channels. At Vector, that eventually became what we called the B2B surround sound play: one core ICP audience, brand awareness on connected TV, retargeting back into LinkedIn engagement ads and thought leadership, plus a Google search layer to capture the demand the awareness campaigns were creating. We wrote up that exact play in [a separate blog](https://www.vector.co/blog/vector-on-vector-the-surround-sound-play-that-turned-15k-into-41-more-pipeline) if you want the actual mechanics.

You don’t have to copy that structure. But the principle to steal is layered campaigns built on a shared audience, not five disconnected campaigns competing for the same budget.

### This is also when you start the signal conversation.

If you’re going to activate signals or run an ABM motion later in the year, the foundation for that work starts now. You don’t have to have a target account list or have a signal architecture finalized yet. You do need to start asking which closed-won deals had which signals present before they closed, because that’s the analysis that builds the list. We’ll go deeper on this in section 9.

Month three is when you stop experimenting and start optimizing. The question shifts from whether anything is working to what to double down on.

### Run an honest retro.

The retro version that helps you is the one where you're willing to kill things that didn't work. The retro version that hurts you is the one designed to make the first 60 days look good.

The questions worth asking:

*   Which campaigns produced pipeline. Which produced engagement without pipeline. Which produced nothing.

*   Which creative is fatiguing. (Creative is fatiguing faster than it used to, more on this in the AI section.)

*   Which channels punched above their weight. Which under-performed and why.

*   Which audiences engaged at higher rates. Which ones I’d retire.

### Plan the next 90.

By the end of month three, you should have enough signal to say what the next quarter looks like. For most teams at this stage, that means doubling down on the channels that worked, starting the signal or ABM motion, and building out a more mature reporting layer.

### The reporting answer at 90 days.

By 90 days, you should have enough to show direction, not enough to defend every dollar. The attribution work takes longer than that, and setting that expectation with leadership early is the same play as telling them in month one to give the platforms time to learn.

**A note on what didn’t survive my own first 90 days**

Full disclosure: a newsletter I'd planned to launch never happened. The ICP refresh I’d planned to own end-to-end became a team project. A bunch of attribution work I’d planned to handle manually moved to a tool because the scope had grown beyond what I should be hand-building. This is a normal part of the job adapting around the work that actually mattered.

Most new demand gen hires inherit a half-built stack. Some of it is essential on day one. Some of it can wait. Knowing the difference is what saves you from buying tools that don’t change your pipeline.

The framework I use is simple. Three layers: what you need to ship, what you’ll need by month two, and what you can wait on entirely. If something doesn’t help you ship work in the next 90 days, it’s probably not a day-one tool.

Day one

*   CRM

*   Ad platforms (1–2 to start)

*   Audience builder

*   Engagement visibility

*   Design resources (freelancer or a tool that helps you ship creative fast)

*   Conversion tracking + basic last-touch attribution

Month Two

*   Reporting tool (offline conversion tracking + customer journey mapping)

Earned it

*   Multi-touch attribution platform (the full purpose-built version)

*   Creative automation tools

*   Dedicated outbound orchestration

### **The Vector layer.**

Two pieces of the foundation above are where Vector fits naturally: an audience builder that doesn’t require you to have a target account list before you can run anything, and engagement visibility that goes beyond “someone clicked, someone didn’t.” Our [ICP Builder](https://www.vector.co/blog/product-release-icp-builder) lets you define your audience by who they actually are. Our [Reveal](https://www.vector.co/product/reveal) product tells you, by name, who clicked your ads and visited your site. Both are things I needed on day one.

The reason I’m putting this in a kit for new demand gen hires (instead of in a list of “later” tools) is that the longer you wait to build the audience layer right, the more budget you spend reaching people you don’t actually want. That’s why this category is foundational for me.

Hot Take

Marketers tend to over-index on tools that help us defend our work, and under-index on tools that help us ship it. If you're choosing between a reporting platform and a tool that gets your ads in front of the right buyers, ship first. Report second. Your pipeline will thank you, and you'll get a lot fewer questions.

![Image 29](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/666c800c0d49f944831ac2e5/6a5592222c850f73e620031d_hot-take-icon-relative.png)

This deserves its own section because it’s where new demand gen hires lose the most time. Here’s the version of the attribution conversation I’d want someone to hand me on day one.

### What you need to launch.

Genuinely minimum. Three things:

*   **Conversion tracking from website to ad platforms.** Tag manager set up, conversion actions defined, UTM parameters defined and taxonomy defined, the basics. If this isn’t in place, fix it before you launch anything

*   **Offline conversion tracking from CRM to ad platforms.** So the ad platforms know when a demo or trial signup became a qualified lead, and when that lead closed. This is what teaches the platforms to find more of your real buyers, so they stop optimizing toward bots or non-ICP form-fillers.

*   **Last-touch and first-touch reporting in your CRM.** Even if it’s basic, like UTM parameters tied to the lead source field. You need to be able to tell a directional story by month two.

### What you can wait on.

Everything else, including the things that probably feel essential right now. Multi-touch attribution. Customer journey mapping. Impression-level account influence. A purpose-built attribution platform. All of these are valuable, but none of them block your first campaign.

01

Need to launch

In-platform conversion tracking

The minimum. If this isn't in place, fix it this week.

02

Need to launch

Offline conversion tracking (CRM → ad platforms)

Teaches the platforms what a real conversion looks like, not just a form fill.

03

Need to launch

Last-touch and first-touch in the CRM

Directional. Doesn't have to be perfect. Enough to tell a story by month two.

04

Build in month 2-3

Multi-touch attribution + influence on pipeline

Customer journey, account-level engagement, ads-influenced-revenue.

05

When you've earned it

A purpose-built attribution platform

Buy when manual lift exceeds the cost of the tool.

### What this looked like for me.

I used in-platform reporting and CRM last-touch for the first 60 days, paired with Google Looker Studio and Supermetrics for the manual reporting work. To the rescue!: Vector MCP

Some of the daily attribution work I was doing manually is now handled by [Vector MCP](https://www.vector.co/abm). Things like campaign pacing, creative fatigue, and which ICP visitors came from which campaigns. I can even pull blended data with other MCPs to understand:

The framework I use thinks about signals in three dimensions. Fit and relevance happen at the company level. Engagement happens at the person level. The most valuable accounts and contacts sit at the intersection of all three.

*   Industry, size, geography

DIMENSION 2

*   New market or region launch

*   For each one, work backward through the signals that were present before they closed. Look across all three dimensions.
*   Build a hypothesis list of signals you’d target. I started with around 35.

Going from 40 to five or six feels brutal. It is. Complex signal architecture is earned over time. Get your wins in with the most important signals.

kept.heading: THE 4 ROLES EVERY MODERN MEASUREMENT FUNCTION NEEDS AND ALMOST NO COMPANY HAS STAFFED ALL 4 (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Modern marketing measurement needs four distinct roles: measurement scientist, experimentation lead, finance translator, and decision architect. The scientist builds trustworthy models, the experimentation lead produces causal evidence, and the finance translator reconciles modeled impact with financial results so finance can trust the numbers. The decision architect connects those findings to budget processes by defining decision rights, timing, and override protocols. Combining roles may work temporarily, but understaffing usually leaves the relationship and decision work undone and turns measurement back into a modeling exercise.

Title: The 4 Roles Every Modern Measurement Function Needs And Almost No Company Has Staffed All 4.

URL Source: https://karandhir.substack.com/p/the-4-roles-every-modern-measurement

Published Time: 2026-08-26T18:01:15+00:00

Markdown Content:
Over the past 3 weeks I have described the operating system of a modern measurement function. The weekly cadence that makes measurement an advisor rather than a historian. The experimentation muscle that generates decisions rather than validating them. The reconciliation layer that converts marketing claims into enterprise numbers. This final piece is about who actually runs that system, because the honest answer at most organizations is that nobody does, and the reason nobody does is a staffing model that was never designed for the function it is supposed to support.

The standard staffing model for marketing measurement is a single senior hire, usually titled some variation of Head of Marketing Analytics or Director of Measurement Science, supported by a small team of analysts. The senior hire is almost always selected for methodological depth. The interview process tests statistical knowledge, modeling experience, and familiarity with the current tooling landscape. The successful candidate is, by construction, a measurement scientist.

Then the organization hands that scientist a mandate that requires 4 different professions. Build the models. Run the experiments. Earn finance’s trust. Change how budget decisions get made. The scientist executes the first mandate excellently, struggles through the second, improvises the third, and never gets to the fourth, because the fourth requires organizational authority and cross-functional fluency that no individual contributor hire arrives with, however senior. 2 years later, the model is technically excellent and strategically irrelevant, the scientist concludes the company was not ready, and the company concludes measurement does not pay. Both parties are correct about the symptoms and wrong about the disease.

The disease is the staffing model. The function requires 4 distinct roles, and I want to describe each one precisely, because the boundaries between them are where most organizations get confused.

_The Measurement Scientist_

The measurement scientist builds and validates the models. This is the role organizations understand, so I will spend the least time on it, except to make 1 point that gets missed: the defining skill of a great measurement scientist is not modeling ability. It is epistemic honesty about what the models can and cannot claim.

The marketing measurement landscape is full of technically proficient modelers who will produce a channel-level ROI estimate for anything, with confidence intervals that imply far more certainty than the underlying data supports. The scientist the function actually needs is the one who says: the model can support this claim at this confidence level, it cannot distinguish between these 2 channels given the data we have, and these 3 estimates should not be used for budget decisions until we validate them experimentally. That discipline is what makes every downstream conversation trustworthy. A measurement function built on a scientist who oversells precision is compromised at the foundation, and no amount of excellence in the other 3 roles repairs it.

_The Experimentation Lead_

The experimentation lead designs and operates the causal testing program. Organizations routinely assume this is the same job as the measurement scientist, and the assumption is wrong in a way that matters.

The scientist’s core skill is extracting signal from observational data. The experimentation lead’s core skill is designing interventions in the live business that produce clean causal answers without breaking anything. These are different disciplines. The experimentation lead needs to negotiate holdout regions with sales leaders who do not want their territories in the control group. They need to size tests against realistic effect distributions, sequence a rolling calendar of experiments so the tests do not contaminate each other, and maintain the pre-committed decision rules that make results binding rather than negotiable. The work is as much operational and diplomatic as it is statistical.

When this seat is empty, the experiments either do not happen or happen badly. Underpowered tests produce ambiguous results that everyone interprets according to their prior position. Poorly negotiated holdouts get overridden mid-test by a regional leader with a quarterly target. The organization concludes that experimentation does not work for a business like theirs, which becomes 1 more piece of institutional folklore protecting the status quo. The models lose their calibration source, and the entire function drifts back toward asserted rather than validated numbers.

_The Finance Translator_

The finance translator owns the reconciliation layer I described last week: the maintained bridge between modeled impact and financial actuals. The role requires genuine bilingualism, and I mean that as a precise description rather than a metaphor.

The translator must understand the model deeply enough to explain, without hedging, why modeled incremental revenue is a counterfactual quantity that will never appear in the general ledger, and must understand financial reporting deeply enough to build the decomposition bridge in terms finance recognizes as legitimate. They must know what a residual is acceptable to disclose and how to investigate one that is not. They must be credible enough in a finance review that when the CFO’s team questions an adjustment, the answer resolves the question rather than escalating it.

Organizations typically attempt to cover this role with either a strong analyst from the measurement team or a finance business partner assigned to marketing. Both fail predictably. The analyst has the model fluency and no standing with finance. The business partner has the standing and no model fluency. The role only works when 1 person holds both, and people with both are rare enough that the organizations serious about this capability develop them internally, usually by embedding a high-potential measurement person inside the finance organization for a rotation, or the reverse. The investment takes a year. The alternative is a measurement function that produces numbers finance politely receives and quietly discounts, which costs more than a year.

_The Decision Architect_

The fourth role is the one that does not exist in most org charts, and it is the role I have spent the largest part of my career performing under other titles. The decision architect connects measurement outputs to the organizational processes where budget actually moves.

The work is specific, even though the title is unfamiliar. The decision architect maps the organization’s decision calendar: which allocation decisions recur, on what cadence, with which participants, requiring what inputs. They design the delivery of measurement findings into those decisions, in the format and at the moment the decision participants can act on them. They negotiate the decision rights: which choices the model informs, which it recommends, and which it decides, with the boundaries agreed before the findings arrive rather than contested after. They run the override protocol, documenting when leaders act against the measurement recommendation and tracking the outcomes, not to punish the overrides but to build the institutional record that makes the next conversation empirical rather than positional.

When this seat is empty, everything upstream becomes decoration. The models are excellent, the experiments are rigorous, finance trusts the numbers, and the findings still arrive as a quarterly readout into a planning process that has already concluded. I have watched this exact configuration at organizations that had invested millions in the first 3 roles. The measurement was true. It was also inert, because nobody owned the connection between the truth and the money.

_Why the 4 Roles Cannot Be Collapsed_

The recurring executive question about this framework is whether a sufficiently talented person can cover 2 or more of the seats, and the honest answer is: occasionally, temporarily, and at a cost that compounds.

The roles conflict in their daily incentives. The scientist’s incentive is precision, which slows everything. The experimentation lead’s incentive is throughput, which pressures rigor. The translator’s incentive is conservatism, because their credibility with finance depends on never being caught overselling. The decision architect’s incentive is influence, which tempts toward overselling. A function with all 4 seats staffed holds these tensions productively, the way a well-constructed leadership team does. A function with 1 person holding 3 seats resolves the tensions inside 1 head, invisibly, and the resolution drifts toward whichever incentive matches that person’s temperament. The organization loses the argument it needed to have.

There is also a scaling reality. At a $1B portfolio, each of these roles is a full workload. The experimentation calendar alone, run properly, consumes a senior person. The reconciliation cadence, run properly, consumes another. Collapsing the seats does not eliminate the work. It rations it, and the rationed work is always the relationship work, because the model refresh has a deadline and the finance coffee does not. The function drifts back toward being a modeling shop, which is exactly the failure mode the staffing model was supposed to prevent.

_What the Complete Function Looks Like_

The organizations that have staffed all 4 roles share a recognizable operating rhythm. The models refresh on the decision calendar, not the research calendar. The experiment pipeline runs continuously, with results feeding model calibration and the reconciliation bridge on a standing schedule. Finance participates in the measurement review rather than receiving its output. And the measurement function sits inside the budget decisions, with agreed decision rights, rather than reporting on them afterward.

From the inside, the most noticeable property is that measurement stops being a department and becomes an operating system. Questions that used to trigger meetings trigger queries of the experimental archive. Allocation debates that used to run on conviction run on the reconciled numbers, with the disagreements narrowing to the genuinely uncertain territory where judgment belongs. The CMO defends the budget to the CFO with numbers the CFO’s own team helped construct. This is what the measurement investment was always supposed to buy, and the reason most organizations never receive it has nothing to do with their models.

The 4-role framework is the most consequential thing I have learned building this function. The models were the easy part. The team design was the part that determined whether any of it mattered.

The series closes here. The weekly cadence, the experimentation muscle, the reconciliation layer, and the talent stack are 1 system. Organizations can adopt the components in sequence, and the sequence I have described across these 4 weeks is the one I would follow. But the destination is a measurement function that participates in every meaningful allocation decision the company makes, with numbers that finance underwrites and a track record the organization can query. The companies that build this will allocate capital better than their competitors every quarter, permanently. That is the entire case, and it has never been stronger than it is right now.

Title: Before declaring “___ is dead”, consider that you may just be boring.

URL Source: https://raisedonsocial.substack.com/p/shot-take-stop-declaring-things-as-dead

Published Time: 2026-08-13T12:32:05+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IcLp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8dc0ad14-d219-4a6b-821b-3d640643dd8a_499x488.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IcLp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8dc0ad14-d219-4a6b-821b-3d640643dd8a_499x488.jpeg)

**Author: Liv Molho, Strategy Manager, [The Goat Agency](https://goatagency.com/)**

I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again: We haven’t had monoculture since kelly clarkson won american idol.

What I mean by that, is that online echo chambers are not just political anymore. Every social media platform is so oversaturated with content from creators, brands and bots, that everyone is experiencing culture in a different way. Even more, different cultures all together.

One through line though, is what I would like to call “**Judgement Currency**“.

Hot takes have become a cultural pandemic. Everyone feels the need to make a conclusion on everything all the time. Everyone is writing a think-piece. Everyone is racing their peers to be the first to predict the next trend, and complete their retrospective on the last one.

Ultimately, what I don’t think people realize is that while their social media “take” may appear thoughtful or clever to some, it is most likely not true for everyone - because other people are on entirely different versions of the internet.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ioiu!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd1aa33f4-43ae-497b-99c7-689c5fd3ed53_600x327.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ioiu!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd1aa33f4-43ae-497b-99c7-689c5fd3ed53_600x327.jpeg)

Don’t get me wrong - I do recognize the irony of writing a think-piece on how think-pieces are killing internet culture. I’m not declaring that they must go away all together. I am just wondering if maybe, we take a step back and make a little more room for nuance. What I’ve been thinking about is **the overconfidence of internet commentary**.

The internet rewards **certainty over curiosity**.

When people are online and see that the influencers, brands, and media contributors in general are giving so much value to cultural declarations like:

“___ is dead”

“___ is in”

“___ is bad”

“___ is back”

Etc… it infiltrates the way people think.

Telling people what to think is a great way to sell products, but is also a great way to keep them from forming their own opinions. Besides the obvious downsides to this, it also disregards the fact that most of the time these cultural conclusions are not actually even true across the wider internet, and therefore start to feel more like **saying things for the sake of having something to say**.

Basically, I think the person declaring that a certain culture/trend is “dead” simply isn’t looking very hard.

One of the strangest things about algorithmic feeds is that they slowly convince us they’re objective. We stop seeing them as personalized recommendations and start treating them like reality. If your TikTok is boring, you assume TikTok is boring. If every creator sounds the same, you conclude creativity is dead. If you’ve seen one too many “deinfluencing” videos, suddenly luxury is over, maximalism is back, skinny jeans are dead again, sincerity is cringe, irony is dead... until next Tuesday.

But your algorithm is not the culture: it’s a mirror. (And it’s reflecting your own habits more than what’s actually happening.)

We consume so much content that we hit diminishing returns incredibly quickly. The fifth creator making a trend feels derivative. The twentieth feels totally unbearable. Eventually, we conclude the trend itself has run its course.

But, that only feels true because we watched those twenty videos in under an hour. Someone else, on an entirely different corner of the internet, is still seeing it for the first time. This matters because marketers, strategists (hi), and creators are especially guilty of treating their own feeds like market research (working on it).

“One of the strangest things about algorithmic feeds is that they slowly convince us they’re objective.”

We spend all day immersed in internet culture. Then we mistake our own exhaustion for everyone else’s. We declare that audiences are tired of something when really _we’re_ tired of something.

Sometimes a format isn’t dead. You’ve just been looking at it for eight hours a day.

So before declaring that something is dead, over, cringe, back, or the future… Ask yourself this question: **is culture actually changing? Or am I just tired of my own feed?**

Our urgency to reach conclusions is making us worse cultural observers. We stop exploring. We stop looking for contradictions. We stop venturing outside our own algorithm long enough to discover that someone else is having an entirely different cultural experience.

Curiosity is infinitely more interesting than certainty, and if you’ve decided you’ve already seen everything the internet has to offer...

You may just be boring.

Title: The Great Meta Migration

URL Source: https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/the-great-meta-migration/

Published Time: 2026-08-26T12:00:23+00:00

Markdown Content:
Meta alumni are on the move – and they’re bringing the world’s most successful ad playbook with them to the next generation of would-be ad platform greats.

OpenAI, the newest ad platform of the bunch, has gone furthest fastest, hiring hundreds of Zuck alums, including former top brass. But it’s not alone. Amazon Ads, TikTok and Roku ([recently acquired by Fox](https://www.adexchanger.com/tv/fox-announces-plans-to-acquire-roku-for-22-billion/)) have all recruited VPs in product and sales with the same name on their resume: Meta.

The appeal of hiring Meta veterans is undeniable. These are the folks who build the _ne plus ultra_ of ad platforms.

Meta’s ad platform is user friendly enough to serve both mom-and-pop advertisers and to (mostly) satisfy massive agency holding companies and picky brands with multimillion-dollar budgets.

Its growth has been staggering. Meta’s once astonishing Series B valuation of $500 million during “The Social Network” era has multiplied 2,000 times since then to a market cap north of $1 trillion.

Even critics have to give Meta its due.

“It pains me to say this, but I think they were one of the best, [most] well-run companies in the industry for the longest time,” said MiQ CMO Jordan Bitterman, a media agency vet who was at Digitas and Mindshare during Meta’s rise.

Now, thanks to turmoil within, Meta employees are more poachable than ever.

Rolling layoffs have made the company feel unstable, not that morale has been all that great since the Cambridge Analytica scandal in 2018. The allure of leaving to join an early-stage platform on the upswing is a temptation that’s hard to resist.

## **The Meta alumni network, featuring OpenAI**

OpenAI has been the most aggressive recruiter, and the most deliberate.

Long before the company officially launched its ads business in February, it hired former Facebook product leader Fidji Simo as its CEO for artificial general intelligence more than two years ago –a signal the ad industry didn’t miss. ([Simo stepped down](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/09/openai-exec-fidji-simo-says-she-will-step-down-and-transition-to-part-time-advisor.html) over the summer to focus on her health, but is still an advisor to OpenAI.)

Meanwhile, David Dugan, OpenAI’s head of global ad solutions, and Benji Shomair, its VP of monetization, both came to the AI platform after logging a dozen years apiece striking Facebook partnerships and building the advertiser customer base. It was Dugan who took the stage in Cannes this summer to formally [introduce the ad world to ChatGPT advertising](https://www.adexchanger.com/ai/at-its-first-ever-cannes-openai-says-we-are-clearly-in-the-advertising-business-now/).

But the senior hires are only part of the story.

As of now, 10% of OpenAI employees list “Meta” somewhere in the experience section of their LinkedIn profile (a rough gauge of how many Meta-to-OpenAI employees exist). The ranks are filled with managers, engineers and mid-level employees from Menlo Park.

That influence is visible in the product.

“The platform looks very, very similar to the old Meta ad manager back in the day,” said Lara Koenig, MiQ VP of global strategy and partnerships, who is keeping close tabs on its buying user interface and capabilities.

To scale as quickly as OpenAI clearly wants to, Koenig said, “you need the simplest platform that is not going to break, and that has new features every day.”

Even OpenAI’s feature development road map – like conversion APIs – feels like a “Meta move,” she added.

## **Amazon Ads grows up**

If OpenAI is the newest devotee of the Meta playbook, then Amazon Ads is the proof of concept.

After years of work, Amazon’s DSP, fueled in part by an influx of Meta talent, has become the envy of the industry: simple and laser-focused on measurable results.

It wasn’t always that way. In the past, Amazon’s platform was roundly criticized for its clunky user interface and incompatible, in-house ad tech. To many, the gap between its potential and the reality signaled either Amazon’s arrogance, cluelessness or perhaps even indifference toward the advertisers sending it billions.

The fix came from outside. Amazon Ads hired numerous industry veterans from other platforms, including ex-Meta VP Kelly MacLean, the executive now leading Amazon’s DSP product and engineering.

“Complexity has always been a feature, not a bug, and I think that needs to be completely reversed,” she said of her work on Amazon’s demand-side platform. Her goal, she said, is to “continue to simplify” the DSP, even as it adds features.

## **TikTok goes its own way**

TikTok, too, has made Meta hires to build its platform.

The app’s VP of product management, David Kaufman, logged three and a half years at Meta and a year more at Google. Blake Chandlee, the company’s former sales lead and president of global business solutions, spent a dozen years at Meta before joining TikTok in 2019.

A LinkedIn count puts the number of ex-Meta employees who now work at TikTok at around 700 – enough to sway the direction of the platform, but a far lower percentage than the ex-Meta crew at OpenAI.

That’s because TikTok’s ambition isn’t to copy Meta; it’s to build a platform that encompasses every other piece of the digital advertising pie, from in-feed ads to search and video, creator advertising and an integrated shop.

“TikTok has everything,” Kaufman said, when asked to compare the platforms. “I think it’s pretty hard to find that span of capability in one unified experience.”

## **Who does Fox hire?**

And then there’s CTV, which has long struggled to attract the mid-market advertisers who are Meta’s bread and butter.

Roku, recently acquired by Fox, is betting it can change that dynamic by also putting a Meta veteran in a top ad role. Patrick Harris, who spent nearly a dozen years at Meta, became Roku’s SVP of advertising and partnerships this spring (by way of a two-year stint at Snap before that).

Smaller advertisers have long been intimidated by TV’s high production costs and complex buying process, your local carpet king or mattress giant notwithstanding.

“CTV platforms are in a race to bring in mid-market and lower-budget ad dollars,” said Sarah Caputo, founder and CEO of strategic marketing consultancy Fraction Method. “These are the barriers the self-service products at Meta and Google were built to compete against,” she said, “[and] ex-Meta are a natural fit to fuel CTV’s next phase of expansion.”

As the big TV programmers roll out their own self-serve ad platforms, they’re being built on the Meta model and, in some cases, by former Meta employees.

## **The talent factory**

Across the history of ad tech, there have been a handful of companies whose alumni went on to do great things across the industry. DoubleClick, Razorfish, Yahoo and AppNexus all incubated many future industry leaders.

Often, internal turbulence has shaken talent loose, and Meta is no exception. It’s faced ongoing morale issues ever since Cambridge Analytica in 2018.

“While Meta’s ad business continues to print money, working inside the company is not the most stable environment,” Caputo said. “Repeated reorgs and flattened models where managers are now running teams of fifty have taken a toll.”

As a result,she added, “Meta has inadvertently created an enormous bench of highly trained talent who know how to build and sell measurable, self-serve ad products, but who are increasingly choosing to leave rather than wait out the next restructuring.”

Bitterman’s assessment was more blunt: “Google does a much better job retaining its employees,” he said.

## **The risk of leaving Meta**

Not that leaving Meta isn’t sometimes a gamble.

Applying the Meta playbook works best if a would-be platform is on an up-and-to-the-right exponential growth trajectory. Folks who left Meta for Pinterest learned this lesson the hard way.

Back when Pinterest was first getting started with its ad platform, the company brought over many Facebook employees eager to work on an early-stage ad platform –and grab the equity that comes along with that mission. Most notably, Tim Kendall, Pinterest’s president for six years, joined from Meta in 2012.

But many of those who migrated from Meta were humbled when it became clear that user growth at Pinterest could not come close to Facebook’s. Some of those early Pinterest employees boomeranged right back to the big blue mother ship.

OpenAI has its sights set on generating $100 billion in ad revenue by 2023 – but [eMarketer thinks](https://www.adweek.com/media/openais-ad-business-is-on-pace-to-miss-its-own-forecast-by-90-analyst-says/) it could miss that target by 90%. An easy-to-use, Meta-inspired ad manager only gets you so far if the underlying platform stalls or the scale isn’t there.

Not that Meta’s dominance was inevitable, even though its success feels like a fait accompli in retrospect. Its ads team navigated pivots that would have sunk a platform with less capable employees. The ads team, in particular, dealt with many thorny situations – the shift from desktop to mobile, the integration of ads to Instagram, managing multiple ad boycotts and the PR crises that came with them – all while keeping ad revenue up double digits quarter after quarter.

That’s why ex-Meta employees are in high demand. They didn’t just build a great ad platform; they kept it great and functioning under pressure.

But two questions remain as the Meta diaspora fans out across the industry: Can Meta retain its dominance even as its employees apply the playbook elsewhere? And will any of these former Meta folks help build the advertising business that will eventually overshadow the social platform that wrote the playbook?

Title: Boots’ reactive marketing strategy capitalises on influencer’s idea to give back to Ariana Grande fans - CORQ

URL Source: https://corq.studio/insights/boots-reactive-marketing-strategy-capitalises-on-influencers-idea-to-give-back-to-ariana-grande-fans/

Markdown Content:
Boots has proved the power of reactive marketing by quickly greenlighting a creator’s idea to invite 22 fans to the closing night of [Ariana Grande’s](https://www.instagram.com/arianagrande)_The Eternal Sunshine Tour_ in London.

Over the weekend, pop culture and concert creator [Sasha Ridge](https://www.tiktok.com/@sasharidge/) turned to [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@sasharidge/video/7676767866053528854) to take a chance and see whether any brands were interested in spending nearly £10,000 on a suite at the O2 for Grande’s tour. Within three hours, Boots replied: “Girl we’re IN. Let’s do this”.

The idea was conceived between Ridge and [Milly](https://www.tiktok.com/@xemilyamelia) (xemilyamelia), who decided on the plan 12 hours before the video was posted on Saturday morning. As Ridge said in her video, “I was like ‘girl, you’re crazy. No brand is gonna do that’ – but they might”. The lesson? You don’t ask, you don’t get.

The original [video](https://www.tiktok.com/@sasharidge/video/7676767866053528854) has 324,800 views, 31,700 likes and 785 comments, and her [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@sasharidge/video/7676861763760966934) reacting to Boots’ comment has 108,200 views. Cumulatively, Milly and Ridge’s [videos](https://www.tiktok.com/@xemilyamelia/photo/7676869318809799958) about [manifesting](https://www.tiktok.com/@xemilyamelia/photo/7677310935312108822)the [suite](https://www.tiktok.com/@sasharidge/video/7676884080461548823) into existence have more than 793,000 views.

The creator told her LinkedIn [audience](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sasharidge_what-an-insane-24-hours-its-been-at-11pm-activity-7497176280015081472-BZOq?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAABv5BLkBTuE07j_OVPR8qS_dHIDKoQ9fh3U): “No campaign brief. No weeks of planning. Just an idea, an incredibly engaged community, and a brand willing to move quickly and say yes.”

Boots’ head of social Emily Bell also explained the [decision](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7497221474307608576/) on LinkedIn: “No planning or lengthy briefing and approval process, just brilliant instinct from the team, a creator with an idea her community wanted to get behind, and a brand willing to move at the speed of social. THIS is what being truly social-first looks like – building the confidence, relationships and ways of working that allow you to react when the right moment appears.”

The high demand for Grande’s _The Eternal Sunshine Tour_ has meant many fans missed out on seeing the artist perform live in the UK for the first time in seven years. London has been the final leg of the tour, with Grande playing ten nights at the O2 until 1 September. Then she is not on the [road](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjekqqjl9qqo) again for a “long, long, long, long time”. Closing night isn’t just the finale of Grande’s time in London – it’s the end of a huge chapter and every Arianator wants to be there.

### You may also like

![Image 1](https://corq.studio/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ariana-grande-insights-150x150-optimized.jpg)[](https://corq.studio/insights/trend-board-ariana-grande-fans-prepare-eternal-sunshine-tour-looks-ahead-of-the-london-residency/)

The fact that Boots is willing to take real fans is driving positive sentiment for the brand. Concert creator [Suzanne Stewart](https://www.tiktok.com/@suzannestewart_/) praised the company and [said](https://www.tiktok.com/@suzannestewart_/video/7677158104810655009): “I already have much stronger association of Boots because they’re actually gonna give the chance to fans for once. And as a brand, the type of content you’ll get from taking real fans to a show, who have the passion [and] know every single song, it just makes you look so much more culturally relevant.” Meanwhile, pop culture commentator [Dan Cash](https://www.tiktok.com/@dancashio?) commented on Ridge’s post: “This is such a great idea!! I always think brands should buy boxes and fill them with real fans.”

There is a rise in influencer fatigue over creators being invited to high-demand tours or sent on lavish brand trips. In the past, brands have been criticised for inviting influencers who are not genuine fans of an artist to a show, as seen with the backlash about creators at [_The Eras Tour_](https://corq.studio/insights/backlash-to-influencer-trips-to-taylor-swifts-eras-tour-prove-brands-need-community-strategy-now/). Instead, creators like [Sophia Tuxford](https://www.instagram.com/sophiatuxford/) and [Cinzia Baylis-Zullo](https://www.instagram.com/cinziabayliszullo/), and [Amelia Olivia](https://www.instagram.com/amelia0livia/), [Channon Mooney](https://www.tiktok.com/@channonmooney?lang=en) and [Grace Alexandra](https://www.instagram.com/gracealexandrra/?hl=en) have been [praised](https://corq.studio/insights/influencer-concert-activations-drive-roi-as-harry-styles-wembley-residency-generates-1-billion-for-london/) for taking their followers to shows like Harry Styles’ _Together, Together_ tour and Olivia Dean’s _The Art of Loving Live_. It’s real-world community building.

Boots’ [reactive strategy](https://corq.studio/insights/analysis-in-brief-reactive-marketing-is-key-as-spam-sends-women-in-spam-founder-a-surprise-mailer/) shows that it is not only invested in Ridge and the Ariana Grande fandom but is an [active participant](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZsOJMdokGE/?hl=en) in cultural events. The way Boots quickly jumped on the opportunity proves it has an always-on social team that’s willing to invest in creators, their audiences and their ideas.

_By Caroline Edwards, trends editor at CORQ._

Q. What’s happening? 

 A. If you have a phrase or exact match kw (e.g. women’s hats) & a broad match kw that’s understood to be equivalent (e.g. ladies hats), & opted into AAR for removing redundant keywords, Google will remove the exact/phrase match kws & keep the broad match.

Q. Why is Google making this change? 

 A. Ease of use. If you already have an equivalent broad match keyword in your account, removing redundant phrase/exact match keywords still allows your ads to appear for those same searches without having to manage those extra keywords.
